title: Single-cell and spatial evidence with biological replication
text:
Biological question and data
Does observing many cells from eight animals provide the same intervention information as observing that many independent animals?
The worked measurements are fictional continuous cell-level values, not an RNA-seq analysis. Treatment is assigned to animals. A supplied animal-specific effect induces within-animal dependence. Animal-mean analysis is used to illustrate that unit; actual single-cell pipelines need count/assay-specific models and sample-level design.
No biological download is required. Numerical inputs are hypothetical, not observed animal data. The runnable examples use base R. Count and abundance units are specified where used.

title: Single-cell and spatial evidence with biological replication
text:
1. Generate nested measurements
Twenty cells belong to each animal. The animal-specific effects are supplied, not independently assigned to cells.


Show R code
set.seed(3101)
animal <- rep(paste0("a",1:8),each=20)
treatment_animal <- rep(c(0,1),each=4)
animal_effect <- c(-1,.5,1,-.5,.8,-.2,1.2,-.8)
dat <- data.frame(animal,treatment=rep(treatment_animal,each=20))
dat$value <- 1+dat$treatment+rep(animal_effect,each=20)+rnorm(160,sd=.2)
c(cells=nrow(dat),animals=length(unique(dat$animal)))


  cells animals 
    160       8 


The dataset has 160 measurements but eight independently treated animals.

title: Single-cell and spatial evidence with biological replication
text:
2. Compare uncertainty at different units
Fit the intentionally naive independent-cell model and a model of animal means. Label the naive fit as unsuitable for the allocation.


Show R code
naive <- lm(value~treatment,dat)
means <- aggregate(value~animal+treatment,dat,mean)
animal_fit <- lm(value~treatment,means)
result <- data.frame(analysis=c("naive independent cells","animal means"),
 estimate=c(coef(naive)["treatment"],coef(animal_fit)["treatment"]),
 SE=c(coef(summary(naive))["treatment","Std. Error"],
 coef(summary(animal_fit))["treatment","Std. Error"]),
 residual_df=c(df.residual(naive),df.residual(animal_fit)))
result


                 analysis estimate        SE residual_df
1 naive independent cells 1.152614 0.1286135         158
2            animal means 1.152614 0.6397319           6


Show R code
stopifnot(nrow(means)==8,result$SE[1]<result$SE[2])


Equal cell counts make the mean contrasts agree, while the independent-cell assumption understates uncertainty. More measurement resolution did not create independent animals.

title: Single-cell and spatial evidence with biological replication
text:
3. Critique additional advanced claims
For each claim identify the measurement, dependence and missing evidence.


Show R code
review <- data.frame(claim=c("adjacent spatial spots interact","AI cell split predicts new animals",
 "chromatin contact proves regulatory direction"),
 question=c("resolution, cell mixtures, spatial dependence and mechanistic evidence?",
 "were animals separated and all preprocessing learned in training?",
 "what perturbation/temporal evidence establishes the causal relationship?"))
review


                                          claim
1               adjacent spatial spots interact
2            AI cell split predicts new animals
3 chromatin contact proves regulatory direction
                                                                  question
1  resolution, cell mixtures, spatial dependence and mechanistic evidence?
2        were animals separated and all preprocessing learned in training?
3 what perturbation/temporal evidence establishes the causal relationship?


These are hypothetical critique prompts. Co-location, prediction and molecular contact describe different kinds of evidence.

title: Single-cell and spatial evidence with biological replication
text:
Interpretation and limits
The example is not a single-cell/spatial software pipeline. Pseudobulk or hierarchical methods must reflect the assay and animal/specimen design. Advanced technology and AI do not remove the need for independent replication, provenance and appropriate validation.

title: Single-cell and spatial evidence with biological replication
text:
Exercises

Why do the point estimates agree here?
Would splitting cells from every animal produce a new-animal prediction test?
What should a critical paper review report?







Suggested answers






Every animal has equal cell counts, so the treatment contrast averages the same animal-level values.
No; animal-specific information appears in both training and test.
Question, measured unit/resolution, replication, processing, model assumptions, evidence strength, alternative explanations and a justified follow-up.

title: Genomic association and regulatory-variation analysis
text:
Biological question and data
Does marker1 associate with the fictional gene01 expression profile after accounting for diet and batch?
The generator supplies a marker1 effect on gene01 log expected expression, as well as diet and batch effects. Animals are unrelated/independent in the model. The supplied exposure is known. The quasi-Poisson working model is not a calibrated GWAS/eQTL pipeline for real related animals.
No biological download is required. Numerical inputs are hypothetical, not observed animal data. The runnable examples use base R. Count and abundance units are specified where used.

title: Genomic association and regulatory-variation analysis
section: 1. Align the counted allele and expression
text:
1. Align the counted allele and expression
The 0/1/2 dosage counts a fictional designated allele. Keep sample IDs and the exposure offset explicit.


Show R code
helper_dir <- if (dir.exists("R")) "R" else "../R"
stopifnot(file.exists(file.path(helper_dir,"teaching_data.R")))
source(file.path(helper_dir,"teaching_data.R"))
d <- teaching_data()
meta <- d$metadata
meta$dosage <- d$genotypes[meta$animal,"marker1"]
meta$count <- as.vector(d$counts["gene01",meta$animal])
meta$exposure <- unname(d$exposure[meta$animal])
stopifnot(all(meta$dosage%in%0:2),qr(model.matrix(~diet+batch+dosage,meta))$rank==4)
table(meta$dosage)



 0  1  2 
24 17  7 


A dosage cannot be called favourable or causal from its numeric coding.

title: Genomic association and regulatory-variation analysis
text:
2. Fit the supplied expression-association model
Use diet, batch, dosage and exposure. Translate the dosage coefficient into expected expression ratio per counted allele.


Show R code
fit <- glm(count~diet+batch+dosage+offset(log(exposure)),data=meta,family=quasipoisson())
tab <- coef(summary(fit))
tab


                Estimate Std. Error   t value     Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)    3.5615999 0.10122556 35.184788 7.373035e-34
dietsupplement 0.6993352 0.09064197  7.715357 1.037504e-09
batchB         0.2401195 0.08424766  2.850163 6.625961e-03
dosage         0.2904990 0.05306185  5.474724 1.983275e-06


Show R code
c(log_effect_per_allele=coef(fit)["dosage"],
 mean_expression_ratio_per_allele=exp(coef(fit)["dosage"]),
 supplied_generator_ratio=exp(.3))


           log_effect_per_allele.dosage mean_expression_ratio_per_allele.dosage 
                               0.290499                                1.337094 
               supplied_generator_ratio 
                               1.349859 


The fitted estimate need not equal exp(.3) in one count realization. The uncertainty belongs to a restricted working variance model, not a qualified biological eQTL analysis.

title: Genomic association and regulatory-variation analysis
section: 3. Create a correlated candidate and examine ambiguity
text:
3. Create a correlated candidate and examine ambiguity
A nearly identical marker can tag the same signal. Genotype correlation is not an independent confirmation.


Show R code
candidate <- meta$dosage
candidate[1] <- (candidate[1]+1)%%3
c(dosage_correlation=cor(meta$dosage,candidate))


dosage_correlation 
         0.9802964 


Show R code
second <- glm(count~diet+batch+candidate+offset(log(exposure)),data=meta,family=quasipoisson())
c(marker1_effect=coef(fit)["dosage"],tagged_candidate_effect=coef(second)["candidate"])


            marker1_effect.dosage tagged_candidate_effect.candidate 
                        0.2904990                         0.2893723 


Show R code
stopifnot(length(candidate)==48)


A correlated candidate can inherit association. Two conditional models here do not calculate a fine-mapping posterior or identify a causal allele.

title: Genomic association and regulatory-variation analysis
text:
Interpretation and limits
Real studies need allele/reference alignment, genotype and expression QC, relatedness/structure treatment, adequate replication, cis/trans definitions, multiple testing and model diagnostics. A TWAS association is not automatically evidence that expression mediates the variant–trait effect. Fine-mapping requires an explicit candidate/model/LD framework.

title: Genomic association and regulatory-variation analysis
text:
Exercises

What is the expected ratio per allele in the generator?
Does a correlated candidate represent another independent biological effect?
What would an expression-mediation claim additionally require?







Suggested answers






exp(.3), about 1.35, conditional on the supplied model.
No; association can be tagged through correlated dosage.
Temporal/causal assumptions and evidence addressing shared genetic and environmental drivers, not merely paired association tests.

title: Microbiome composition and host–microbiome interpretation
text:
Biological question and data
Can a taxon’s relative decrease occur without any absolute decrease, and how should a microbial association with performance be interpreted?
The first table supplies invented absolute quantities. The shared fixture then supplies fictional read counts; these do not identify absolute microbial load or activity. A .5 pseudocount is used only for a sensitivity demonstration, not as a universally valid zero solution.
No biological download is required. Numerical inputs are hypothetical, not observed animal data. The runnable examples use base R. Count and abundance units are specified where used.

title: Microbiome composition and host–microbiome interpretation
text:
1. Compare absolute and relative changes
Increase one component while keeping the others fixed.


Show R code
absolute <- rbind(before=c(A=10,B=10,C=10),after=c(A=20,B=10,C=10))
relative <- absolute/rowSums(absolute)
relative


               A         B         C
before 0.3333333 0.3333333 0.3333333
after  0.5000000 0.2500000 0.2500000


Show R code
stopifnot(absolute[1,"B"]==absolute[2,"B"],relative[2,"B"]<relative[1,"B"])


B decreases in proportion because A increased. The fraction alone cannot diagnose absolute depletion.

title: Microbiome composition and host–microbiome interpretation
text:
2. Inspect a hypothetical read panel
Normalize within each sample and verify that fractions sum to one.


Show R code
helper_dir <- if (dir.exists("R")) "R" else "../R"
stopifnot(file.exists(file.path(helper_dir,"teaching_data.R")))
source(file.path(helper_dir,"teaching_data.R"))
d <- teaching_data()
counts <- d$microbial
fraction <- sweep(counts,2,colSums(counts),"/")
stopifnot(max(abs(colSums(fraction)-1))<1e-12,
 identical(colnames(fraction),d$metadata$animal))
barplot(fraction[,1:8],col=rainbow(nrow(fraction)),ylab="Relative read fraction",
 xlab="Fictional animals",legend.text=rownames(fraction))









Relative read representation combines biology and measurement. Extraction and assay properties affect what is observed.

title: Microbiome composition and host–microbiome interpretation
section: 3. Examine a log ratio and zero sensitivity
text:
3. Examine a log ratio and zero sensitivity
Use taxon01/taxon02 with explicit pseudocount values. A ratio removes a common multiplicative sample factor for positive components.


Show R code
ratio <- log((counts[1,]+.5)/(counts[2,]+.5))
c(response_correlation=cor(ratio,d$metadata$response))


response_correlation 
         -0.03721842 


Show R code
zero_case <- c(A=0,B=10)
pseudocount <- c(.1,.5,1)
data.frame(pseudocount,log_ratio=log((zero_case["A"]+pseudocount)/(zero_case["B"]+pseudocount)))


  pseudocount log_ratio
1         0.1 -4.615121
2         0.5 -3.044522
3         1.0 -2.397895


The zero-case ratio depends materially on the pseudocount. A host correlation in this panel is a descriptive association, not a microbial intervention result.

title: Microbiome composition and host–microbiome interpretation
text:
Interpretation and limits
Distinguish amplicon/shotgun methods, site, time, diet, contaminants, compositionality and load. The fixture does not model a real rumen community. Cross-layer network or methane claims require identified measurements and suitable designs.

title: Microbiome composition and host–microbiome interpretation
text:
Exercises

Why cannot fractions recover total microbial load?
What assumption is hidden in a pseudocount?
What could confound a taxon–production association?







Suggested answers






Multiplying all absolute quantities by the same factor preserves fractions.
It supplies an artificial positive value for an unobserved/zero component, whose effect depends on scale and detection process.
Diet, management, host genotype, sampling site/time and technical processing.

title: Integrated multi-omics interpretation and alternative explanations
text:
Biological question and data
When two molecular layers associate with the same production response, what can be concluded?
Proteins, metabolites and response share a deliberately supplied latent factor. Diet and genotype also contribute. The measured features are not specified as direct causes of the response in the generator.
No biological download is required. Numerical inputs are hypothetical, not observed animal data. The runnable examples use base R. Count and abundance units are specified where used.

title: Integrated multi-omics interpretation and alternative explanations
section: 1. State the evidence at its measurement level
text:
1. State the evidence at its measurement level
Align one protein, one metabolite and the response, all in the same animals.


Show R code
helper_dir <- if (dir.exists("R")) "R" else "../R"
stopifnot(file.exists(file.path(helper_dir,"teaching_data.R")))
source(file.path(helper_dir,"teaching_data.R"))
d <- teaching_data()
meta <- d$metadata
z <- data.frame(protein=d$protein[1,],metabolite=d$metabolite[1,],response=meta$response,
 diet=meta$diet,batch=meta$batch,dosage=d$genotypes[meta$animal,"marker1"])
round(cor(z[,1:3]),2)


           protein metabolite response
protein       1.00       0.24     0.16
metabolite    0.24       1.00     0.21
response      0.16       0.21     1.00


Cross-layer agreement is an observed covariance pattern. It is not independent replication because the same animals and common driver contribute.

title: Integrated multi-omics interpretation and alternative explanations
text:
2. Account for supplied measured covariates
Compare raw correlation with correlation of residuals after adjustment for diet, batch and genotype dosage.


Show R code
rp <- residuals(lm(protein~diet+batch+dosage,z))
rm <- residuals(lm(metabolite~diet+batch+dosage,z))
c(raw=cor(z$protein,z$metabolite),after_measured_adjustment=cor(rp,rm))


                      raw after_measured_adjustment 
                0.2367859                 0.2053569 


Show R code
stopifnot(length(rp)==48,length(rm)==48)


The unmeasured part of the latent factor remains shared. Adjustment can change the pattern without identifying a mechanistic direction.

title: Integrated multi-omics interpretation and alternative explanations
section: 3. Connect claims to a suitable next study
text:
3. Connect claims to a suitable next study
Distinguish prediction, response and mechanism before selecting follow-up.


Show R code
follow_up <- data.frame(claim=c("predict new animals","diet changes a molecular profile","protein mediates performance"),
 next_step=c("validate full pipeline in eligible new animals",
 "appropriate allocated contrast with assay/batch checks",
 "temporal and perturbation evidence with explicit mediation assumptions"))
follow_up


                             claim
1              predict new animals
2 diet changes a molecular profile
3     protein mediates performance
                                                               next_step
1                         validate full pipeline in eligible new animals
2                 appropriate allocated contrast with assay/batch checks
3 temporal and perturbation evidence with explicit mediation assumptions


More omics layers may strengthen a description without resolving the key uncertainty. A targeted experiment can be more informative than another correlated panel.

title: Integrated multi-omics interpretation and alternative explanations
text:
Interpretation and limits
Conditional correlations do not rule out unmeasured confounding, measurement error, reverse causation or selection. A mediation claim needs temporal ordering and justified assumptions, not simply a smaller diet coefficient after adding a molecular covariate.

title: Integrated multi-omics interpretation and alternative explanations
text:
Exercises

Why is layer agreement not independent replication here?
Does a residual correlation prove direct interaction?
What should a null or inconsistent layer result contribute?







Suggested answers






The same animals and deliberately common generating driver supply both measurements.
No; an unmeasured common cause can remain.
It constrains the explanation and should be reported, with assay sensitivity and context considered.

title: Integrated analysis and comparison of prediction strategies
text:
Biological question and data
Does integration add predictive information beyond either hypothetical molecular layer alone?
The split, penalty and integration weights are supplied. No test outcome chooses a feature, penalty or mixture weight. The fixture is a small illustrative simulation; all responses use arbitrary units.
No biological download is required. Numerical inputs are hypothetical, not observed animal data. The runnable examples use base R. Count and abundance units are specified where used.

title: Integrated analysis and comparison of prediction strategies
text:
1. Specify the competing strategies
Compare separate protein/metabolite ridge models, weighted early concatenation and a fixed average of separate predictions.


Show R code
helper_dir <- if (dir.exists("R")) "R" else "../R"
stopifnot(file.exists(file.path(helper_dir,"teaching_data.R")))
source(file.path(helper_dir,"teaching_data.R"))
d <- teaching_data()
source(file.path(helper_dir,"prediction_helpers.R"))
P <- t(d$protein);M <- t(d$metabolite);X <- cbind(P,M)
y <- d$metadata$response;train <- 1:32;test <- 33:48
stopifnot(identical(rownames(P),rownames(M)))
models <- list(protein=fit_teaching_ridge(P[train,],y[train]),
 metabolite=fit_teaching_ridge(M[train,],y[train]),
 early=fit_teaching_ridge(X[train,],y[train],weights=c(rep(1/sqrt(ncol(P)),ncol(P)),
 rep(1/sqrt(ncol(M)),ncol(M)))))
stopifnot(max(abs(models$protein$center-colMeans(P[train,])))<1e-12)


Weights are applied after training standardization in the helper. Re-standardizing the weighted columns would cancel these intended block weights.

title: Integrated analysis and comparison of prediction strategies
text:
2. Predict without using test outcomes
The late strategy uses a prespecified equal average. It is not a test-optimized ensemble.


Show R code
prediction <- cbind(protein=predict_teaching_ridge(models$protein,P[test,]),
 metabolite=predict_teaching_ridge(models$metabolite,M[test,]),
 early=predict_teaching_ridge(models$early,X[test,]))
prediction <- cbind(prediction,late=rowMeans(prediction[,c("protein","metabolite")]),
 baseline=mean(y[train]))
error <- sweep(prediction,1,y[test],"-")
data.frame(strategy=colnames(prediction),test_RMSE=sqrt(colMeans(error^2)))


             strategy test_RMSE
protein       protein  1.319743
metabolite metabolite  1.244327
early           early  1.215457
late             late  1.242978
baseline     baseline  1.348718


Show R code
stopifnot(nrow(prediction)==length(test),all(is.finite(prediction)))


All strategies face the same animals and loss. The comparison can show whether the selected strategy helps in this realization, rather than assuming more layers must improve performance.

title: Integrated analysis and comparison of prediction strategies
text:
3. Inspect a paired comparison
Subtract squared errors animal by animal. Inspect variability, not just a ranking.


Show R code
improvement <- error[,"protein"]^2-error[,"early"]^2
c(mean_paired_MSE_improvement=mean(improvement),
 animals_improved=sum(improvement>0),animals_evaluated=length(improvement))


mean_paired_MSE_improvement            animals_improved 
                   0.264384                    8.000000 
          animals_evaluated 
                  16.000000 


Show R code
plot(y[test],prediction[,"early"],pch=19,xlab="Observed response",ylab="Early-integration prediction")
abline(0,1,col="#d95f02")









Positive improvement means smaller squared error for early integration than the protein model. The sign can differ across animals and seeds.

title: Integrated analysis and comparison of prediction strategies
text:
Interpretation and limits
The source contains a restricted educational ridge helper, not a general modelling package. One farm-composition split cannot qualify an operational predictor. Nested tuning, independent cohorts, calibration, measurement availability and costs belong in a real comparison.

title: Integrated analysis and comparison of prediction strategies
text:
Exercises

Why does the fixed late average avoid one kind of leakage?
How would you choose mixture weights legitimately?
Why might adding a layer worsen prediction?







Suggested answers






Test outcomes do not choose the weight.
Estimate/tune them in training-only validation, then freeze the pipeline before evaluation.
Noise, small samples, redundant features, shift or unsuitable scaling/regularization can outweigh added information.

title: Multi-omics integration with matched samples and balanced blocks
text:
Biological question and data
What changes when protein and metabolite layers are integrated rather than inspected separately?
The 48 animals have complete matched log2 measurements in these two layers. A shared latent factor was deliberately used to generate them. PCA is descriptive; its full-sample transformation is not used as a prediction evaluation.
No biological download is required. Numerical inputs are hypothetical, not observed animal data. The runnable examples use base R. Count and abundance units are specified where used.

title: Multi-omics integration with matched samples and balanced blocks
text:
1. Align layers before integration
Keep biological IDs visible and check them against metadata.


Show R code
helper_dir <- if (dir.exists("R")) "R" else "../R"
stopifnot(file.exists(file.path(helper_dir,"teaching_data.R")))
source(file.path(helper_dir,"teaching_data.R"))
d <- teaching_data()
P <- t(d$protein);M <- t(d$metabolite)
stopifnot(identical(rownames(P),d$metadata$animal),identical(rownames(P),rownames(M)))
c(protein_features=ncol(P),metabolite_features=ncol(M),animals=nrow(P))


   protein_features metabolite_features             animals 
                  8                   6                  48 


An assay match requires the right animal and sampling context, not just equal matrix dimensions.

title: Multi-omics integration with matched samples and balanced blocks
text:
2. Scale features and weight blocks
Standardize each feature. Then divide each block by the square root of its feature count so its total marginal variance is one.


Show R code
ZP <- scale(P);ZM <- scale(M)
balanced <- cbind(ZP/sqrt(ncol(P)),ZM/sqrt(ncol(M)))
c(protein_total_variance=sum(apply(ZP/sqrt(ncol(P)),2,var)),
 metabolite_total_variance=sum(apply(ZM/sqrt(ncol(M)),2,var)))


   protein_total_variance metabolite_total_variance 
                        1                         1 


Show R code
stopifnot(abs(sum(apply(ZP/sqrt(ncol(P)),2,var))-1)<1e-12,
 abs(sum(apply(ZM/sqrt(ncol(M)),2,var))-1)<1e-12)
fit <- prcomp(balanced,center=FALSE,scale.=FALSE)
head(fit$sdev^2/sum(fit$sdev^2))


[1] 0.57637485 0.07750314 0.07220047 0.05527056 0.04574651 0.03833449


Equal total marginal variance is a specified weighting choice. It does not assert equal information, independence or biological importance.

title: Multi-omics integration with matched samples and balanced blocks
section: 3. Inspect the representation and shared association
text:
3. Inspect the representation and shared association
Label scores by the biological design and calculate one paired cross-layer association.


Show R code
plot(fit$x[,1],fit$x[,2],col=as.integer(d$metadata$diet),pch=19,
 xlab="Joint PC1",ylab="Joint PC2")
legend("topleft",levels(d$metadata$diet),col=1:2,pch=19,bty="n")









Show R code
c(cross_layer_correlation=cor(P[,1],M[,1]))


cross_layer_correlation 
              0.2367859 


The panels can agree because they share the same generating driver. In actual data, biological and technical common causes both need examination.

title: Multi-omics integration with matched samples and balanced blocks
text:
Interpretation and limits
Concatenation is one integration strategy, not a universal method. Unmatched samples, incompatible timing, missing layers and leakage need explicit handling. Do not interpret joint PCs as mechanisms or use full-sample scaling for an untouched predictive test.

title: Multi-omics integration with matched samples and balanced blocks
text:
Exercises

What happens without the block weights?
Does matching animal IDs establish matching tissue/time?
Are correlated layers independent replications?







Suggested answers






The eight standardized protein features contribute more marginal variance than the six metabolite features.
No; specimen metadata must confirm context.
Not generally; shared samples, drivers and processing can create dependence.

title: Exploratory multi-omics analysis and principal components
text:
Biological question and data
Which sample patterns appear in the hypothetical protein and metabolite panels?
Animals are rows in the PCA inputs; molecular features are columns. Both panels are supplied log2 values and contain shared latent variation by construction. Standardization is used for description, not prediction.
No biological download is required. Numerical inputs are hypothetical, not observed animal data. The runnable examples use base R. Count and abundance units are specified where used.

title: Exploratory multi-omics analysis and principal components
text:
1. Prepare matched feature matrices
Use complete measurements and explicit animal alignment.

X <- cbind(P,M)
fit <- prcomp(X,center=TRUE,scale.=TRUE)
variance_fraction <- fit$sdev^2/sum(fit$sdev^2)
head(variance_fraction)

title: Metabolomics processing, standards and feature interpretation

Biological question and data
How does an internal standard help distinguish instrument drift from a supplied concentration pattern?
The first calculation has an ideal shared drift factor affecting analyte and standard equally. The fixture metabolite table is already log2 arbitrary abundance; its feature labels do not identify actual compounds.
No biological download is required. Numerical inputs are hypothetical, not observed animal data. The runnable examples use base R. Count and abundance units are specified where used.

1. Test an ideal measurement correction
An analyte and a standard are multiplied by the same hypothetical response factor.

Allow analyte response to vary differently from the standard.

Biological question and data
How should an individually allocated diet study collect molecular profiles and later performance measurements?
The hypothetical design allocates diet to individual animals. Pen-allocated diets would require a different unit and replication plan. The practical specifies metadata and tests design identifiability; it does not establish sample size or a collection protocol for a real assay.

3. Plan decision timing and missingness

title: Multi-omics experimental design in animal production

Interpretation and limits
Randomization and blocking, tissue/time, sex, farm, batch, handling and exclusion rules need a justified study-specific plan. Technical aliquots are not independent animals. Use NC3Rs design guidance for the design principles; the invented sheet is not a laboratory sampling instruction.

Biological question and data
What evidence and processing record should accompany a computational result?
The example fits a simple animal-level response model to fictional data. Diet allocation, independence and the chosen covariates are assumptions of this teaching design. The report records a conditional estimate, not a livestock recommendation.
No biological download is required. Numerical inputs are hypothetical, not observed animal data. The runnable examples use base R. Count and abundance units are specified where used.

title: Scientific reporting and reproducible analysis records
text:
Interpretation and limits
A real report needs species/population, measurement units, design, permissions, assay processing, software, missingness, diagnostics, validation and uncertainty. Tables and plots should allow readers to assess the conclusion without relying on an unexplained significant/not-significant label.

A specific molecular mechanism or a dependable effect in another farm/population.
Selection may bias the estimate; document and justify exclusions and assess sensitivity.
Methods, variable definitions, provenance, permissions/access process and a non-sensitive reproducible demonstration.

Correlation can reflect diet, genotype, tissue mixture, batch or other common drivers. A network inferred from abundance is not equivalent to a curated interaction database. 3. Fit the mean model and report uncertainty
Fit each gene with diet, batch and a log-exposure offset. The diet coefficient uses the natural-log link; divide it and its standard error by log(2) to obtain log2 units.

 fit <- glm(y~diet+batch+offset(log(exposure)),data=meta,family=quasipoisson())
 tab <- coef(summary(fit))

 SE_log2=tab["dietsupplement","Std. Error"]/log(2),
 p_value=tab["dietsupplement","Pr(>|t|)"],
 variance_multiplier=summary(fit)$dispersion)
}
result <- as.data.frame(t(apply(counts,1,fit_gene)))
result$BH <- p.adjust(result$p_value,"BH")

result$lower <- result$log2_effect-qt(.975,model_df)*result$SE_log2
result$upper <- result$log2_effect+qt(.975,model_df)*result$SE_log2

title: RNA-seq counts, contrasts and uncertainty
text:
Interpretation and limits
This practical teaches design, exposure, contrasts and uncertainty; it is not a production differential-expression pipeline. The DESeq2 workflow adds composition-aware normalization and a gene-level negative-binomial dispersion framework. Gene filtering, relatedness, batch design and larger-scale validation need explicit decisions for real data.

title: RNA-seq counts, contrasts and uncertainty
text:
Exercises

What supplied log2 effect corresponds to .65 on the natural-log scale?
Why is Poisson variance too restrictive for these generated counts?
Change the seed and explain why estimates and adjusted p-values change.
What would a complete treatment–batch confounding problem prevent?
Why might normalized counts still show batch separation in PCA?
Convert the gene01 estimate and interval to abundance ratios and write a result sentence.
Does selecting a gene at BH < .05 establish a 95% probability that its diet effect is real?
Why should an unusual residual trigger inspection of records before exclusion?







Suggested answers






.65/log(2), about .94; a finite-sample estimate need not equal it.
The generating variance is mu + mu squared/12, greater than mu.
Sampling realization changes, while the generating parameters remain the same.
Separate estimation of diet and batch effects.
Exposure adjustment changes the count scale; it does not remove systematic batch differences.
Use 2^estimate, 2^lower and 2^upper; describe the supplement-versus-control tissue-level comparison conditional on batch and the working model.
No. The BH procedure addresses false discovery rate across a family of tests under its assumptions, not an individual posterior probability.
An unusual observation may be biological, technical or a model discrepancy. Exclusion needs an independently justified reason and a sensitivity assessment.

title: Protein structure and structural bioinformatics
text:
Biological question and data
Which residue pairs lie close together in a supplied protein-coordinate model?
The six coordinates are invented C-alpha positions in angstroms, not a protein database structure. Euclidean proximity is calculated under a supplied cutoff; consecutive residues are excluded from the contact summary.
No biological download is required. Numerical inputs are hypothetical, not observed animal data. The runnable examples use base R. Count and abundance units are specified where used.

title: Protein structure and structural bioinformatics
text:
1. Inspect coordinates and distances
Rows represent residues. Distance is calculated in the stated coordinate system.


Show R code
xyz <- rbind(c(0,0,0),c(3.8,0,0),c(7.6,0,0),c(7.6,3.8,0),c(3.8,3.8,0),c(0,3.8,0))
rownames(xyz) <- paste0("residue",1:6)
D <- as.matrix(dist(xyz))
round(D,2)

residue1     0.00     3.80     7.60     8.50     5.37     3.80
residue2     3.80     0.00     3.80     5.37     3.80     5.37
residue3     7.60     3.80     0.00     3.80     5.37     8.50
residue4     8.50     5.37     3.80     0.00     3.80     7.60
residue5     5.37     3.80     5.37     3.80     0.00     3.80
residue6     3.80     5.37     8.50     7.60     3.80     0.00


Show R code
stopifnot(abs(D[1,2]-3.8)<1e-12,isSymmetric(D))


The folded-back hypothetical geometry places some non-neighbour positions near each other.

title: Protein structure and structural bioinformatics
text:
2. Define a contact rule
A distance below five angstroms is a teaching cutoff. Exclude immediate sequence neighbours and diagonal entries.


Show R code
contact <- D<5 & abs(row(D)-col(D))>1
pairs <- which(contact & upper.tri(contact),arr.ind=TRUE)
data.frame(residue1=rownames(D)[pairs[,1]],residue2=colnames(D)[pairs[,2]],
 distance_A=D[pairs])


  residue1 residue2 distance_A
1 residue2 residue5        3.8
2 residue1 residue6        3.8


Show R code
stopifnot(nrow(pairs)==2)
image(1:6,1:6,contact,xlab="Residue index",ylab="Residue index",
 col=c("white","#1b9e77"),main="Supplied geometric contact rule")









Contacts describe geometry under the chosen threshold. They are not measured interactions or binding energies.

title: Protein structure and structural bioinformatics
text:
3. Assess threshold dependence
Count contacts at several cutoffs using the same non-neighbour rule.


Show R code
cutoffs <- c(4,5,8)
data.frame(cutoff_A=cutoffs,contacts=vapply(cutoffs,function(cut)
 sum((D<cut & abs(row(D)-col(D))>1)[upper.tri(D)]),integer(1)))


  cutoff_A contacts
1        4        2
2        5        2
3        8        8


A contact list changes when its operational definition changes.

title: Protein structure and structural bioinformatics
text:
Interpretation and limits
For an actual structure, record accession, model, chain, residue numbering, units, experimental/predicted status and structural uncertainty. A C-alpha cutoff is an abstraction; side chains, ligands, solvent and conformational dynamics affect biological interpretation.

What changes when coordinates are converted to nanometres?
Why exclude sequential neighbours?
Does a contact establish functional necessity?







Suggested answers






Values divide by ten and the cutoff must also divide by ten.
They reflect backbone proximity and can obscure non-local geometry.
No; perturbation and functional evidence are needed.

title: Alignment and conserved-region analysis
text:
Biological question and data
How do alignment and missingness decisions change the apparent conservation of a region?
The local helper uses Needleman–Wunsch global alignment with fixed match, mismatch and linear-gap scores. The multiple alignment is supplied, not inferred by this pairwise helper.
No biological download is required. Numerical inputs are hypothetical, not observed animal data. The runnable examples use base R. Count and abundance units are specified where used.

title: Alignment and conserved-region analysis
section: 1. Align two sequences under stated scores
text:
1. Align two sequences under stated scores
Global alignment compares the entire supplied sequences. Different scoring choices can change an optimal alignment.


Show R code
helper_dir <- if (dir.exists("R")) "R" else "../R"
stopifnot(file.exists(file.path(helper_dir,"sequence_helpers.R")))
source(file.path(helper_dir,"sequence_helpers.R"))
a <- "ACGTACGT"; b <- "ACGACGT"
fit <- global_alignment(a,b)
fit


$a
[1] "ACGTACGT"

$b
[1] "ACG-ACGT"

$score
[1] 12


Show R code
stopifnot(gsub("-","",fit$a)==a,gsub("-","",fit$b)==b,
 nchar(fit$a)==nchar(fit$b),fit$score==12)
self <- global_alignment(a,a)
stopifnot(self$score==2*nchar(a),self$a==a,self$b==a)


Seven matches and one gap produce a score of 12 under +2/−1/−2 scoring. The score is not an evolutionary distance.

title: Alignment and conserved-region analysis
text:
2. Inspect an existing multiple alignment
A column is conservatively called conserved only when every sequence supplies a nucleotide and all those nucleotides match.


Show R code
aligned <- c(s1="ACGTACGT",s2="ACG-ACGT",s3="ACGTTCGN")
M <- do.call(rbind,strsplit(aligned,""))
called <- M%in%c("A","C","G","T"); dim(called) <- dim(M)
fully_called <- colSums(called)==nrow(M)
conserved <- apply(M,2,function(z) all(z%in%c("A","C","G","T")) && length(unique(z))==1)
data.frame(position=seq_len(ncol(M)),fully_called,conserved)


  position fully_called conserved
1        1         TRUE      TRUE
2        2         TRUE      TRUE
3        3         TRUE      TRUE
4        4        FALSE     FALSE
5        5         TRUE     FALSE
6        6         TRUE      TRUE
7        7         TRUE      TRUE
8        8        FALSE     FALSE


Show R code
stopifnot(sum(fully_called)==6,sum(conserved)==5)


A gap and an unknown base are excluded from fully called columns; a genuine nucleotide difference breaks conservation in another column.

title: Alignment and conserved-region analysis
text:
3. Compare denominators
Calculate both the fraction of all alignment columns and the fraction of fully called columns that are conserved.


Show R code
c(conserved_of_all=sum(conserved)/ncol(M),
 conserved_of_fully_called=sum(conserved)/sum(fully_called))


         conserved_of_all conserved_of_fully_called 
                0.6250000                 0.8333333 


These fractions answer different questions. Report the denominator and missingness rather than choosing the larger value.

Interpretation and limits
The example does not identify an actual functional element. Conservation depends on alignment quality, phylogenetic diversity and evolutionary processes. Production multiple aligners and evolutionary conservation models need their own method choices and diagnostics.

text:
Exercises

Change the gap score and inspect the result.
Why is N not evidence for a conserved base?
Why does conservation alone not prove function?







Suggested answers






Alternative alignments can become optimal, particularly where mismatch and gap alternatives compete.
Its nucleotide is unknown.
Context, species sampling, evolutionary constraints and biological evidence determine the interpretation.

title: Command-line bioinformatics and reproducible execution
text:
Biological question and data
Can the same file-processing task run independently of an interactive R session?
This portable exercise launches the Rscript executable belonging to the current R installation. It requires no Unix shell or external bioinformatics program. It illustrates the command-line interface pattern used by larger tools.
No biological download is required. Numerical inputs are hypothetical, not observed animal data. The runnable examples use base R. Count and abundance units are specified where used.

title: Command-line bioinformatics and reproducible execution
section: 1. Create a small input and worker script
text:
1. Create a small input and worker script
Both files live in a fresh temporary directory. The script takes exactly one input argument and validates it.


Show R code
work <- tempfile("cli-example-"); dir.create(work)
input <- file.path(work,"sample counts.csv")
write.csv(data.frame(sample=c("s1","s2","s3"),count=c(10,20,30)),input,row.names=FALSE)
worker <- file.path(work,"summarise.R")
writeLines(c('args <- commandArgs(trailingOnly=TRUE)',
 'stopifnot(length(args)==1L, file.exists(args[1]))',
 'd <- read.csv(args[1])',
 'stopifnot(all(c("sample","count") %in% names(d)))',
 'cat(sum(d$count), "\n")'),worker)
readLines(worker)


[1] "args <- commandArgs(trailingOnly=TRUE)"               
[2] "stopifnot(length(args)==1L, file.exists(args[1]))"    
[3] "d <- read.csv(args[1])"                               
[4] "stopifnot(all(c(\"sample\",\"count\") %in% names(d)))"
[5] "cat(sum(d$count), \""                                 
[6] "\")"                                                  


Explicit arguments make the worker independent of objects in the current global environment.

title: Command-line bioinformatics and reproducible execution
text:
2. Run and capture the process
Quote each path as a separate argument, including the intentionally spaced input filename.


Show R code
executable <- file.path(R.home("bin"),if(.Platform$OS.type=="windows") "Rscript.exe" else "Rscript")
output <- system2(executable,args=c("--vanilla",shQuote(worker),shQuote(input)),
 stdout=TRUE,stderr=TRUE)
status <- attr(output,"status"); if(is.null(status)) status <- 0L
c(status=status,total=as.numeric(tail(output,1)))


status  total 
     0     60 


Show R code
stopifnot(status==0L,as.numeric(tail(output,1))==60)


The worker reports 60 and exits successfully. Locale-startup messages may appear before the final number on some systems.

title: Command-line bioinformatics and reproducible execution
text:
3. Describe the workflow boundary
Record executable, arguments, input and expected output before applying this pattern to another tool.


Show R code
record <- data.frame(step="sum counts",executable=basename(executable),
 input=basename(input),output="stdout total",expected_total=60)
record


        step  executable             input       output expected_total
1 sum counts Rscript.exe sample counts.csv stdout total             60


For a real aligner, include reference, version, options, resource requirements and the meaning of each output. A zero exit code does not certify biological correctness.

Interpretation and limits
Use tool-specific documentation for real aligners or quantifiers; this example runs no alignment. Keep restricted data out of command logs and public repositories. Temporary files are left in R’s temporary directory for inspection.

Which check remains necessary after a successful exit?

Spaces must stay within one argument.

Which biological records are needed to connect a measured feature to its sequence and annotation? This offline exercise uses fictional records so retrieval is reproducible and does not depend on a live service.
Records are distinct objects; study, sample, gene and transcript identifiers are not interchangeable. Real retrieval needs species, assembly, version and access checks.

1. Inspect the resource catalogue
Use the record type to determine what a query returns.

Select explicitly and round-trip a temporary CSV. This represents retrieval from a supplied snapshot, not an API call.

title: Reproducibility, data governance and responsible research
text: Document provenance and exclusions; distinguish access control from reproducibility; evaluate privacy, research integrity and responsible AI use.

title: Reproducibility, data governance and responsible research
text:
1. Biological question and measurements
Reproducibility means that the documented inputs and procedures can produce the reported analysis. It requires traceable data versions, sample definitions, transformations, software, random draws and model choices. A script that runs is only part of this record: excluded samples, manual corrections and selection decisions affect the result.
A public teaching example can use hypothetical data while a real collaboration may need controlled access. Genetic, ownership, location or linked production records can carry sensitive information. Permissions, consent or institutional agreements determine what may be shared; changing names alone does not necessarily prevent re-identification. Publish reusable methods and non-sensitive demonstrations without transferring restricted records into public repositories.
Responsible AI use includes identifying what the tool contributed and verifying code, citations and interpretations. Do not upload restricted data to an external service without the applicable authorisation. Specific governance decisions depend on the project’s agreements and local requirements.

title: Reproducibility, data governance and responsible research
text:
2. Model and assumptions
A manifest connects a file identifier, checksum, role and access category. A checksum can detect byte-level changes; it cannot determine whether a biological measurement or label is correct. Separate data provenance from biological validity.
An analysis record should distinguish prespecified decisions from exploratory choices and document deviations. Fixing a seed preserves one random realization; it does not establish that findings generalize.

title: Reproducibility, data governance and responsible research
text:
3. Worked example
The inputs below are hypothetical. Run the example, predict one change, then compare your prediction with the result. All executable code uses base R.


Show R code
path <- tempfile(fileext=".csv")
write.csv(data.frame(animal=c("fictional_a1","fictional_a2"),value=c(3,5)),
 path,row.names=FALSE)
manifest <- data.frame(role="hypothetical teaching input",checksum=unname(tools::md5sum(path)),
 access="public synthetic",unit="animal")
manifest


                         role                         checksum           access
1 hypothetical teaching input ca1fa9541bfb9f91c7a0cced0ac7f804 public synthetic
    unit
1 animal


Show R code

unlink(path) # Removes only the temporary file created in this example.


The manifest identifies bytes of one fictional teaching table. A different formatting or row order can change the checksum even when the scientific content is equivalent.

title: Reproducibility, data governance and responsible research
text:
4. Interpretation and scope
Keep credentials, private observations and restricted metadata out of public teaching sources. Report validation and limitations plainly, including null or inconsistent results. Reproducibility does not guarantee correct inference, responsible access or scientific validity.

text:
5. Exercises

Does an unchanged checksum certify correct animal identity?
What should be shared when data access is restricted?
Why record an exploratory feature-selection decision?







Suggested answers






No; it only certifies the same file bytes under the checksum mechanism.
Methods, metadata descriptions, access procedures and an appropriately non-sensitive example, subject to the governing agreements.
Selection affects uncertainty and replication; readers need to know how the analysis was chosen.

title: Integrating molecular layers and phenotypes
text: Distinguish early, intermediate and late integration; align samples and scales; evaluate common latent patterns, missing layers and validation.

title: Integrating molecular layers and phenotypes
text:
1. Biological question and measurements
Integration combines evidence across measurements to answer a defined question. Early integration concatenates compatible features before analysis. Intermediate strategies construct joint representations or relate layer-specific representations. Late integration combines outputs such as predictions or evidence summaries. Choice depends on matching, sample size, measurement process and the biological task.
Verify animal identity, specimen and time before computing cross-layer associations. Samples from the same animal but different time points are not automatically interchangeable. A missing layer can depend on disease severity or technical failure, so a complete-case subset may not represent the target population. Feature scaling controls the influence of units and variance; block weighting also controls the influence of unequal feature counts.

title: Integrating molecular layers and phenotypes
text:
2. Model and assumptions
For layer matrices \(X_k\) with animals in rows, a simple concatenation is \(X=[w_1 Z_1,\ldots,w_K Z_K]\), where \(Z_k\) uses training-derived centering/scaling. Choosing \(w_k=1/\sqrt{p_k}\) gives each standardized block the same total marginal variance p-weight in training when it has \(p_k\) nonconstant features. It is a design choice, not a universally optimal integration method.
Correlated layers may share biology, batch effects or repeated measurements. Cross-layer agreement is not independent replication by default.

title: Integrating molecular layers and phenotypes
text:
3. Worked example
The inputs below are hypothetical. Run the example, predict one change, then compare your prediction with the result. All executable code uses base R.


Show R code
set.seed(1501)
z <- rnorm(12)
A <- cbind(z+rnorm(12,sd=.2), z+rnorm(12,sd=.2))
B <- cbind(z+rnorm(12,sd=.3), rnorm(12), rnorm(12))
ZA <- scale(A); ZB <- scale(B)
combined <- cbind(ZA/sqrt(ncol(ZA)),ZB/sqrt(ncol(ZB)))
fit <- prcomp(combined,center=FALSE,scale.=FALSE)
c(A_total_variance=sum(apply(ZA/sqrt(2),2,var)),
 B_total_variance=sum(apply(ZB/sqrt(3),2,var)),
 PC1_fraction=fit$sdev[1]^2/sum(fit$sdev^2))


A_total_variance B_total_variance     PC1_fraction 
       1.0000000        1.0000000        0.7082201 


Show R code
stopifnot(abs(sum(apply(ZA/sqrt(2),2,var))-1)<1e-12)


Each block has total marginal variance one, but the joint PCs still depend on covariance. The common latent variable was deliberately supplied; a principal component is not a discovered mechanism.

title: Integrating molecular layers and phenotypes
text:
4. Interpretation and scope
An integration example must specify the unit, timing, transformation, missingness policy, target and validation. The MultiAssayExperiment documentation illustrates explicit mappings between assay columns and biological subjects; these practicals implement small analogous checks with base R.

Why can a large feature block dominate concatenated PCA?
Does block weighting remove batch effects?
Where should scaling be estimated for prediction?







Suggested answers






More standardized features contribute more total variance.
No; weighting changes influence, not confounding.
Within each training split, then applied to held-out animals.

title: Association, prediction and regulatory evidence
text: Define marker dosage and phenotype contrasts; identify confounding and linkage disequilibrium; distinguish GWAS, eQTL, TWAS, fine-mapping and prediction.

title: Association, prediction and regulatory evidence
text:
1. Biological question and measurements
GWAS evaluates association between variants and a phenotype. An eQTL analysis evaluates association between variants and expression. TWAS uses expression-related genetic information in a trait-association framework. These approaches connect measurements, but none automatically identifies a causal variant, causal gene or mediation mechanism.
Relatedness and population structure can induce association when genetic groups differ in environment or phenotype. Linkage disequilibrium allows a marker to tag nearby variation; multiple correlated associations need not imply multiple mechanisms. Fine-mapping compares candidate explanations under an explicit model and requires appropriate LD, coverage, allele alignment and prior assumptions. A posterior probability is conditional on that model and supplied candidates.
Genomic prediction evaluates the ability to predict new animals, rather than selecting the smallest association p-value. The deployment population and training relationships determine the relevant validation design.

title: Association, prediction and regulatory evidence
text:
2. Model and assumptions
A basic unrelated-sample model is \(y_i=\beta_0+\beta_g g_i+\gamma^T c_i+e_i\), where \(g_i\) counts a stated allele and c contains prespecified covariates. Residual independence and the design matter. With correlated relatives, a mixed-model or other suitable framework is needed.
For two marker vectors, their correlation describes association of the supplied dosages. It does not establish ancestry, phase, a causal allele or a calibrated fine-mapping probability.

title: Association, prediction and regulatory evidence
text:
3. Worked example
The inputs below are hypothetical. Run the example, predict one change, then compare your prediction with the result. All executable code uses base R.


Show R code
set.seed(1301)
ancestry <- rep(c(0,1),each=20)
g <- rbinom(40,2,ifelse(ancestry==0,.2,.8))
y <- 3*ancestry+rnorm(40)
unadjusted <- lm(y~g)
adjusted <- lm(y~g+ancestry)
c(unadjusted_marker=coef(unadjusted)["g"],adjusted_marker=coef(adjusted)["g"])


unadjusted_marker.g   adjusted_marker.g 
         1.44495380         -0.02545743 


Show R code
stopifnot(qr(model.matrix(adjusted))$rank==3)
plot(g,y,col=ifelse(ancestry==0,"#1b9e77","#d95f02"),pch=19,
 xlab="Counted-allele dosage",ylab="Hypothetical phenotype")









The generating model contains no direct marker effect. Group differences can nevertheless create a marginal marker association. One realization does not make the adjusted estimate exactly zero.

title: Association, prediction and regulatory evidence
text:
4. Interpretation and scope
Adjustment can reduce specified confounding but cannot guarantee that all confounding has been measured. Do not infer causality from conditional association, a TWAS signal or agreement between assays. Fit and validate appropriate models before applying any teaching formula to related livestock data.

Why can a variant associate with a trait without changing it?
What is the eQTL response variable?
Why can randomly splitting relatives exaggerate deployment performance?

LD with causal variation or association with ancestry/environment can produce the signal.
A specified expression measurement in a stated tissue/context.
Close relatives in training and test can make the task easier than prediction in a new family or population.

title: Phenomics, sensors and measurement timing
text: Define phenotypes and units; distinguish repeated observations from independent animals; align sensor measurements to biological sampling and decision times.

title: Phenomics, sensors and measurement timing
text:
1. Biological question and measurements
Phenomics can describe production, behaviour, physiology and environmental response across animals and time. Sensors create dense records, but the biological quantity still needs definition. A daily average, total, slope and within-day variability answer different questions. Document units, calibration, missing coverage and the interval represented by each summary.
When aligning a molecular sample with sensor data, decide whether the intended feature is a pre-sampling baseline, concurrent response or future outcome. A model for day-30 prediction cannot use day-45 sensor records at deployment. Aggregation can also hide short-lived events and differences in monitoring duration.

title: Phenomics, sensors and measurement timing
text:
2. Model and assumptions
For animal i observed at \(n_i\) times, \(\bar y_i=\sum_t y_{it}/n_i\) is a mean over those recorded times, not necessarily the mean over the entire target period. Missing times need a coverage policy.
Under equal marginal variance \(\sigma^2\) and equal within-animal correlation \(\rho\), \(\mathrm{Var}(\bar y_i)=\sigma^2[1+(n_i-1)\rho]/n_i\). Additional correlated records improve precision more slowly than independent records.

title: Phenomics, sensors and measurement timing
text:
3. Worked example
The inputs below are hypothetical. Run the example, predict one change, then compare your prediction with the result. All executable code uses base R.


Show R code
n <- c(1,5,20)
rho <- .6
variance <- (1+(n-1)*rho)/n
data.frame(records=n,variance_of_mean=variance)


  records variance_of_mean
1       1             1.00
2       5             0.68
3      20             0.62


Show R code
set.seed(1101)
records <- data.frame(animal=rep(c("a1","a2","a3"),each=5),
 day=rep(1:5,3), value=rep(c(8,10,12),each=5)+rnorm(15,sd=.4))
aggregate(value~animal,subset(records,day<=3),mean)


  animal     value
1     a1  7.726248
2     a2 10.086693
3     a3 12.094211


The variance approaches the correlation component rather than zero as repeated records accumulate. The summary intentionally uses days 1–3, demonstrating a defined time window.

title: Phenomics, sensors and measurement timing
text:
4. Interpretation and scope
The equal-correlation model is a teaching simplification; actual serial correlation, drift, unequal coverage and animal-level variation need appropriate modelling. Neither millions of sensor rows nor precise technology automatically establish millions of experimental units.

text:
5. Exercises

What happens to variance when rho is zero?
Why should each animal’s monitoring coverage be reported?
Which records are eligible for a prediction made on day 3?







Suggested answers






It is sigma squared divided by n.
Means from different windows or selective missing times may not be comparable.
Information observed by day 3; later records are eligible only as outcomes or in a different task.

title: Metabolite features, identification and quantification
text: Distinguish analytical features from confirmed metabolites; evaluate internal standards and scaling; separate concentration changes from relative signal differences.

title: Metabolite features, identification and quantification
text: Distinguish analytical features from confirmed metabolites; evaluate internal standards and scaling; separate concentration changes from relative signal differences.

title: Metabolite features, identification and quantification
text:
1. Biological question and measurements
Metabolomics measures small molecules using platforms with different coverage and selectivity. A detected feature may describe a mass/charge and retention-time signal rather than a confidently identified compound. Adducts, isotopes and fragments can yield multiple features associated with one molecule. Conversely, co-eluting compounds can complicate a signal.
Targeted assays can quantify defined compounds with calibrations; untargeted assays often yield relative intensities with varying identification confidence. Processing should document blanks, technical QC samples, drift, batches, detection limits and normalization. A table heading called concentration does not turn an arbitrary instrument signal into an absolute chemical measurement.

title: Metabolite features, identification and quantification
text:
2. Model and assumptions
If the observed signal is \(x_{ij}=a_j c_{ij}\) and an internal standard has known concentration \(c_s\) and the same multiplicative factor \(a_j\), the ratio \(x_{ij}/s_j\) cancels that factor. This works only to the extent that the standard tracks the relevant measurement process.
Scaling a feature to mean zero and variance one changes its contribution to a multivariate analysis. It does not convert arbitrary units into comparable concentrations.

title: Metabolite features, identification and quantification
text:
3. Worked example
The inputs below are hypothetical. Run the example, predict one change, then compare your prediction with the result. All executable code uses base R.


Show R code
concentration <- c(2,3,4)
drift <- c(.8,1.1,1.4)
signal <- concentration*drift
standard <- 5*drift
ratio <- signal/standard
data.frame(concentration,signal,standard,ratio)


  concentration signal standard ratio
1             2    1.6      4.0   0.4
2             3    3.3      5.5   0.6
3             4    5.6      7.0   0.8


Show R code
stopifnot(max(abs(5*ratio-concentration))<1e-12)


The common drift cancels in this deliberately idealised example. If the analyte and standard respond differently to preparation or the instrument, that cancellation will be incomplete.

title: Metabolite features, identification and quantification
text:
4. Interpretation and scope
Chemical identity should have documented supporting evidence; a feature ID is not a metabolic pathway assignment. Avoid counting several signals from the same compound as independent confirmations. See the EMBL-EBI metabolite-identification lesson for the distinction between a detected signal and an assigned compound.

title: Metabolite features, identification and quantification
text:
5. Exercises

Why is a feature ID insufficient for a pathway claim?
Under what assumption does the standard correction work?
Why can unit-variance scaling amplify noisy features?







Suggested answers






The compound may not be established; mass, retention and additional chemical evidence need evaluation.
Analyte and standard share the specified multiplicative response.
Each retained feature is given similar variance weight, even when its original variation reflects measurement noise.

title: Epigenomic measurements and regulatory interpretation
text: Distinguish methylation proportions, chromatin-accessibility measurements and expression; evaluate coverage, tissue composition and regulatory claims.

title: Epigenomic measurements and regulatory interpretation
text:
1. Biological question and measurements
Epigenomic assays measure selected properties of DNA and chromatin. Bisulfite-based methylation assays estimate methylated cytosines under conversion and mapping assumptions. Accessibility assays measure the representation of accessible regions under their own sampling process. Neither is a direct universal measure of gene activity. An epigenomic profile is tied to tissue, developmental stage, cellular composition and collection conditions.
Nutritional or environmental exposure can associate with a regulatory measurement. To claim an exposure causes a regulatory change, consider allocation and confounding; to claim that change mediates a phenotype, additional assumptions and evidence are needed. Genotype can affect both a regulatory measurement and the response. Sampling tissue after disease or production changes can also reverse the apparent direction of explanation.

title: Epigenomic measurements and regulatory interpretation
text:
2. Model and assumptions
A simple methylation summary is \(\widehat{p}=m/(m+u)\), where m and u are methylated and unmethylated reads at a supplied site. Under independent binomial sampling of reads conditional on a true proportion p, \(\mathrm{Var}(\widehat p)=p(1-p)/n\). This conditional measurement model does not describe all biological variability between animals; read depth is not the number of independent animals.
A pooled tissue proportion can change when cell-type proportions change even if methylation within each cell type remains constant.

title: Epigenomic measurements and regulatory interpretation
text:
3. Worked example
The inputs below are hypothetical. Run the example, predict one change, then compare your prediction with the result. All executable code uses base R.


Show R code
cell_methylation <- c(typeA=.2,typeB=.8)
composition <- rbind(control=c(.8,.2),treated=c(.3,.7))
pooled <- as.vector(composition %*% cell_methylation)
data.frame(group=rownames(composition), pooled_methylation=pooled)


    group pooled_methylation
1 control               0.32
2 treated               0.62


Show R code
stopifnot(abs(pooled[1]-.32)<1e-12, abs(pooled[2]-.62)<1e-12)
n <- c(10,100)
data.frame(reads=n,conditional_SE=sqrt(.5*.5/n))


  reads conditional_SE
1    10      0.1581139
2   100      0.0500000


The pooled proportion differs by .30 with no within-cell-type change. Increasing read depth reduces conditional sampling error, not the need for biological replication.

title: Epigenomic measurements and regulatory interpretation
text:
4. Interpretation and scope
Conversion efficiency, assay specificity, mapping, coverage and cell composition need evaluation. Conventional bisulfite signals do not by themselves separate every cytosine modification. Technical proportions and production traits can be associated without a direct regulatory mechanism. Sequence and assay context must accompany an epigenomic coordinate.

title: Epigenomic measurements and regulatory interpretation
text:
5. Exercises

Did either cell type change methylation in the example?
Does sequencing one animal 100 times create 100 treatment replicates?
How could sampling time affect a regulatory interpretation?







Suggested answers






No; the mixture changed.
No; these are measurements of one animal, not independent allocations.
A profile measured after a phenotype changes can reflect its consequences rather than its antecedent causes.

title: Genomic measurements and sequence analysis
text: Distinguish sequence reads, assemblies, alignments and genotype calls; calculate simple quality and distance summaries; distinguish similarity from homology and association from mechanism.

title: Genomic measurements and sequence analysis
text:
Biological question and measurements
Sequencing produces reads from molecules, not a finished genome. Assembly reconstructs sequence relationships; alignment compares reads or sequences against a reference; variant calling estimates differences under measurement and calling assumptions. Genotyping platforms measure selected variants. Genome assembly and annotation versions define the coordinates and biological interpretation.
A FASTA record stores a sequence with a header. FASTQ adds per-base quality information. A gap in an alignment represents an alignment decision about an insertion/deletion, not a fifth nucleotide. A SNP dosage of 0, 1 or 2 counts the stated allele in a diploid genotype and requires a missing-call convention.
Identity describes matching aligned residues. Homology describes common ancestry; it is not a percentage. Sequence similarity is evidence to interpret alongside length, complexity, significance and biological context.

title: Genomic measurements and sequence analysis
text:
Model and assumptions
For an aligned comparison with n comparable sites and k differences, \(p=k/n\) is the observed mismatch fraction. Under the Jukes–Cantor assumptions of equal base frequencies and equal substitution rates, \(d=-3/4\log(1-4p/3)\) estimates substitutions per site for \(p<3/4\). Alignment uncertainty and saturation limit this model.
For a Phred quality Q, the encoded error probability is \(10^{-Q/10}\). Summing these probabilities gives an expected number of errors, without assuming the errors are independent.

title: Genomic measurements and sequence analysis
text:
Worked example
The inputs below are hypothetical. Run the example, predict one change, then compare your prediction with the result. All executable code uses base R.


Show R code
Q <- c(10,20,30,40)
data.frame(Q=Q,error_probability=10^(-Q/10))


   Q error_probability
1 10             1e-01
2 20             1e-02
3 30             1e-03
4 40             1e-04


Show R code
a <- strsplit("ACGTACGTACGT","")[[1]]
b <- strsplit("ACGTTCGTTCGT","")[[1]]
p <- mean(a!=b)
d <- -.75*log(1-4*p/3)
c(observed_fraction=p, JC_distance=d)


observed_fraction       JC_distance 
        0.1666667         0.1884858 


Show R code
stopifnot(abs(p-2/12)<1e-12, d>p)


The correction exceeds the observed difference because multiple changes can occur at a site. These short hypothetical sequences do not establish ancestry or a reliable divergence estimate.

title: Genomic measurements and sequence analysis
text:
Interpretation and scope
Whole-genome workflows need species/reference selection, coverage, mapping and calling diagnostics, filtering and assessment of sampling. A clustering tree from distances is not automatically a species phylogeny. Review NCBI’s BLAST glossary for the distinction between identity and homology.

Why is the denominator comparable sites rather than all supplied characters?
Why can a dosage of 2 not be interpreted before specifying the counted allele?
Can a high-identity short alignment establish function?

Gaps and unknown bases do not supply called nucleotide comparisons.
Two counts refer to a particular allele, not a universally favourable genotype.
No; coverage, complexity, evolutionary relationship and functional evidence matter.

title: Biological databases and identifier mapping
text:
Biological question and measurements
A database record is not interchangeable with an organism, a sample or a gene. A study can contain many specimens, and a gene can have multiple transcripts and protein products. Sequence, expression, protein, structure and pathway resources answer different questions. Preserve species, genome assembly, accession/version, coordinate conventions and retrieval date alongside a record.
In a real project, select the organism and assembly before mapping variants to genes. Check whether a downloaded table reports gene IDs, transcript IDs, symbols or probes. Symbols can change or be shared. Joining on an ambiguous display label can duplicate rows or silently lose records. GEO, for example, distinguishes sample, series and platform records; these are different levels of metadata.

title: Biological databases and identifier mapping
text:
Model and assumptions
If feature f maps to several transcripts, a join produces several annotation rows for the same measured value. This is a representation of a relationship, not new biological replication. An eligible pathway background should be constructed from features that could have entered the analysis, after documenting the feature-to-gene mapping.
Check key uniqueness, unmatched records and row expansion before summarising. Define whether many features per gene will be combined, selected or retained; different choices answer different questions.

title: Biological databases and identifier mapping
text:
Worked example
The inputs below are hypothetical. Run the example, predict one change, then compare your prediction with the result. All executable code uses base R.


Show R code
features <- data.frame(gene=c("geneA","geneB","geneC"), effect=c(.5,-.2,.1))
annotation <- data.frame(gene=c("geneA","geneA","geneB"),
 transcript=c("txA1","txA2","txB1"))
joined <- merge(features, annotation, by="gene", all.x=TRUE)
joined


   gene effect transcript
1 geneA    0.5       txA1
2 geneA    0.5       txA2
3 geneB   -0.2       txB1
4 geneC    0.1       <NA>


Show R code
c(input_rows=nrow(features), joined_rows=nrow(joined),
 unmatched=sum(is.na(joined$transcript)))


 input_rows joined_rows   unmatched 
          3           4           1 


Show R code
stopifnot(nrow(joined)==4, sum(is.na(joined$transcript))==1)


geneA appears twice because it has two annotation records. geneC remains present but unmatched. Neither situation should be hidden by a convenient merge.

title: Biological databases and identifier mapping
text:
Interpretation and scope
The fictional labels demonstrate cardinality rather than actual annotation. The same symbol in another species or assembly need not denote the same record. Biological assignment of a nearby variant to a gene is evidence to investigate, not proof of the causal gene. For actual record types, use the NCBI GEO documentation.

Why did the row count increase?
What happens with an inner join?
Name four metadata fields needed for a genomic coordinate.







Suggested answers






geneA has a one-to-many mapping.
geneC disappears; this is an exclusion that should be reported.
Species, assembly, chromosome and coordinate convention; also record the annotation/version and feature identity.

title: Biological questions and omics measurements
text:
Biological question and measurements
A study of feed efficiency can ask whether a diet changes animal performance, whether molecular profiles predict later performance, or which biological mechanisms mediate a change. These questions require different designs. A response to an allocated diet is an intervention contrast; association of a protein with performance is an observational relationship; prediction asks how well a model performs for new animals.
Genomics records sequence variation, transcriptomics records RNA abundance, proteomics records proteins, metabolomics records small molecules, microbiomics describes microbial communities, and phenomics describes traits measured across animals and time. Epigenomic assays describe selected regulatory measurements. Each layer samples a tissue, time and measurement process. A genotype need not predict a transcript in every tissue, and transcript abundance need not determine protein abundance.
Begin with the animal, the exposure, the sampling unit and the decision. Measuring more layers does not compensate for a poorly specified question.

title: Biological questions and omics measurements
text:
Model and assumptions
Let \(Y_i(1)\) and \(Y_i(0)\) denote the performance that animal i would show under two diets. The average intervention effect is \(E[Y(1)-Y(0)]\). Only one potential outcome is observed for each animal. Random allocation can support estimating this contrast; an observational correlation \(\mathrm{cor}(X,Y)\) generally cannot.
For prediction, specify the target population and prediction time. Molecular measurements collected after the response occurs may help explain biology but cannot automatically support an earlier management decision.

title: Biological questions and omics measurements
text:
Worked example
The inputs below are hypothetical. Run the example, predict one change, then compare your prediction with the result. All executable code uses base R.


Show R code
plan <- data.frame(layer=c("genome", "transcriptome", "proteome", "phenome"),
 measurement=c("genotype dosage", "RNA counts", "protein abundance", "feed-efficiency phenotype"),
 timing=c("baseline", "day 14", "day 14", "days 1-28"),
 purpose=c("inherited variation", "molecular response", "molecular response", "production response"))
plan


          layer               measurement    timing             purpose
1        genome           genotype dosage  baseline inherited variation
2 transcriptome                RNA counts    day 14  molecular response
3      proteome         protein abundance    day 14  molecular response
4       phenome feed-efficiency phenotype days 1-28 production response


The table exposes a timing problem: day-14 assays cannot be treated as baseline predictors of the entire days-1–28 outcome without defining a different prediction task.

title: Biological questions and omics measurements
text:
Interpretation and scope
An integrated explanation remains a hypothesis unless the design and analysis support its causal interpretation. Tissue composition, environment, measurement error and reverse causation can produce associations. A smaller, well-designed set of measurements may answer the question better than an indiscriminate panel.

title: Biological questions and omics measurements
text:
Exercises

Define one diet-effect question and one prediction question.
Which measurements would be available before a breeding decision?
Why is agreement between RNA and protein not proof of mediation?







Suggested answers






Compare average responses under allocated diets; separately predict a future phenotype in new animals.
Only information observed at the stated decision time is eligible.
Both can respond to an unmeasured common cause or changes in cell composition.

title: Experimental design and biological sampling
text:
Biological question and measurements
For an individually allocated diet, the animal can be the experimental unit. If a diet is allocated to pens, animals within a pen are not independent diet allocations: the pen is the unit for the intervention. Sequencing lanes, aliquots and repeated measurements are technical or within-unit observations, not additional biological replicates.
A multi-omics study should connect animal identity to tissue, collection time, storage, extraction, assay and batch. Collection and preservation requirements differ across molecules; a shared animal identifier does not imply that one preparation is appropriate for every assay. Predefine exclusion rules and the primary contrast. Where possible, randomise treatment allocation, blind handling and distribute biological groups across processing batches.

title: Experimental design and biological sampling
text:
Model and assumptions
A simple fixed-effect model is \(y_i=\beta_0+\beta_T T_i+\beta_B B_i+e_i\). Its design matrix X must have independent columns to separate treatment and batch. If every control is in batch A and every treatment in batch B, the two effects are not separately identifiable. Increasing the number of observations in the same confounded arrangement does not solve this.
Blocking balances treatments within a known nuisance factor; batch adjustment models remaining variation. Neither creates the missing comparisons in a perfectly confounded design.

title: Experimental design and biological sampling
text:
Worked example
The inputs below are hypothetical. Run the example, predict one change, then compare your prediction with the result. All executable code uses base R.


Show R code
balanced <- data.frame(treatment=factor(rep(c("control","treated"),4)),
 batch=factor(rep(c("A","A","B","B"),2)))
confounded <- transform(balanced, batch=treatment)
rank_info <- function(d) {
 X <- model.matrix(~ treatment + batch, d)
 c(columns=ncol(X), rank=qr(X)$rank)
}
rbind(balanced=rank_info(balanced), confounded=rank_info(confounded))


           columns rank
balanced         3    3
confounded       3    2


Show R code
stopifnot(qr(model.matrix(~treatment+batch, balanced))$rank==3,
          qr(model.matrix(~treatment+batch, confounded))$rank==2)


The balanced design supplies independent treatment and batch columns. The confounded model has three columns but only rank two: software cannot recover the absent information.

title: Experimental design and biological sampling
text:
Interpretation and scope
Rank is necessary, not sufficient, for a good experiment. Power, within-unit dependence, transport/storage effects, selection and missingness still matter. Plan biological replication using a relevant effect size and variance, not a universal sample-count rule. See the NC3Rs experimental-unit guidance for examples.
