title: Programming and reproducible data handling
text:
Biological question and measurements
A reproducible script specifies inputs, transformations, analysis and outputs. Begin by deciding which dimension contains features and which contains samples. In this course assay matrices have features in rows and animals in columns; genotype matrices have animals in rows. Metadata has one row per animal. These choices must be checked every time an object is transformed.
Use stable keys, not row position, to align data. Keep raw records separate from derived tables. Record transformations and exclusions. Relative paths within an RStudio project make examples portable; temporary files should stay in temporary directories. R is the main environment. Command-line and Python exercises introduce portable concepts without making them dependencies of every practical.

title: Programming and reproducible data handling
text:
Model and assumptions
Suppose an assay column is labelled \(a_j\) and metadata row i has animal ID \(m_i\). Alignment is the explicit index \(j_i=\mathrm{match}(m_i,a)\), followed by reordering and an identity check. A missing index means that animal has no matching measurement. Duplicate keys make the mapping ambiguous.
A successful join does not establish that labels are biologically correct. Identity tracking during collection is still necessary.

title: Programming and reproducible data handling
text:
Worked example
The inputs below are hypothetical. Run the example, predict one change, then compare your prediction with the result. All executable code uses base R.


Show R code
metadata <- data.frame(animal=c("a1","a2","a3"), diet=c("C","T","C"))
assay <- matrix(1:6,2,3,dimnames=list(c("f1","f2"),c("a3","a1","a2")))
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(metadata$animal), !anyDuplicated(colnames(assay)))
index <- match(metadata$animal,colnames(assay))
stopifnot(!anyNA(index))
aligned <- assay[,index,drop=FALSE]
stopifnot(identical(colnames(aligned),metadata$animal))
aligned


   a1 a2 a3
f1  3  5  1
f2  4  6  2


Animal a1 now receives its labelled measurement, not the value in the original first column. Keeping drop=FALSE preserves matrix shape when selecting a single column.

title: Programming and reproducible data handling
text:
Interpretation and scope
Checking dimensions alone misses permutations. A seed records a simulation draw, but software versions, inputs, processing choices and model assumptions also affect reproducibility. ID checks cannot detect a correctly labelled tube containing the wrong biological specimen.

What does match return for an absent animal?

It binds by position and can attach measurements to the wrong animals.
NA; require an explicit missing-sample policy before continuing.
Names preserve which units and transformations each object represents, reducing accidental reuse of a processed value as raw data.

title: Transcriptomics and expression analysis
text:
1. Biological question and measurements
Bulk RNA-seq measures RNA from a mixture of cells in a sampled tissue. Read counts depend on abundance, sequencing depth, transcript properties and processing. A difference can arise from expression within a cell type, a change in cell composition, technical effects or combinations of these. Biological replicates are independent experimental units, not reads or genes.
Prepare count matrices and sample metadata with matching IDs. Inspect library sizes and count distributions, define low-information filters independently of a desired direction, and specify the biological contrast and adjustment factors before testing. Expression transformations for visualization are not substitutes for an inferential count model.

title: Transcriptomics and expression analysis
text:
2. Model and assumptions
A negative-binomial model can write \(K_{gj}\sim NB(\mu_{gj},\alpha_g)\) with \(E[K]=\mu\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(K)=\mu+\alpha_g \mu^2\). A known exposure \(s_j\) enters through \(\mu_{gj}=s_j q_{gj}\). Gene-level models describe \(q\) using treatment and other design terms. Dispersion describes extra variation beyond a Poisson model.
The worked calculation uses supplied exposure, not an estimated RNA-seq normalization method. On real data, composition-aware normalization, dispersion estimation, model design and multiplicity require an appropriate workflow.

title: Transcriptomics and expression analysis
text:
3. Worked example
The inputs below are hypothetical. Run the example, predict one change, then compare your prediction with the result. All executable code uses base R.


Show R code
mu <- c(10,100,1000)
alpha <- .1
data.frame(mean=mu,Poisson_variance=mu,NB_variance=mu+alpha*mu^2)


  mean Poisson_variance NB_variance
1   10               10          20
2  100              100        1100
3 1000             1000      101000


Show R code
counts <- c(80,120,160)
exposure <- c(.8,1.2,1.6)
normalized <- counts/exposure
normalized


[1] 100 100 100


Show R code
stopifnot(all(normalized==100))


Equal normalized counts can arise from different read depths. At high mean, the overdispersion term dominates Poisson variance; treating biological count data as Poisson can underestimate uncertainty.

title: Transcriptomics and expression analysis
text:
4. Interpretation and scope
CPM and log2(count+1) are useful teaching transformations but have composition and low-count limitations. The DESeq2 vignette describes a full gene-level count-model workflow. Our base-R practical explores supplied exposure and a restricted quasi-Poisson model; it is not a replacement for its dispersion and normalization framework.

title: Transcriptomics and expression analysis
text:
9. Exercises

A supplement doubles an immune marker in bulk liver tissue. Give two biological explanations and an additional measurement that could distinguish them.
Why do 30 million reads from one animal not give 30 million biological replicates?
In the composition example, what changes if gene A rises to 900 while B and C stay at 100?
With \(\alpha=.1\), what happens to the coefficient of variation as expected count becomes very large?
Why does a treatment coefficient of .65 correspond to about .94 log2 units rather than .65?
Can a PCA plot establish that batch adjustment has removed every technical effect?
Explain why a gene with adjusted p-value .04 should not be described as having a 4% probability of being a false result.
Draft a two-sentence result that gives direction, effect size, uncertainty and the tissue-level scope of interpretation.







Suggested answers






More immune cells or more RNA per immune cell could produce the difference. Cell-type measurements or a suitably designed cell-resolved assay would add evidence.
Reads measure one sample; they do not reproduce the treatment allocation or biological variation between animals.
B’s fraction falls from 1/3 to 1/11, although its absolute abundance is unchanged.
It approaches \(\sqrt{.1}\), about .316. The dispersion component remains.
The fitted log link uses natural logarithms; conversion divides by \(\log(2)\).
No. PCA is descriptive and emphasizes dominant variation; unrecorded effects may remain.
FDR concerns a discovery procedure across tests, not a posterior probability for that individual hypothesis.
For example: “The fitted supplemented-versus-control abundance ratio for this liver transcript was 1.8, with a model-based 95% interval from 1.2 to 2.7 after batch adjustment. This tissue-level association does not distinguish changes in cell mixture from changes within cells.” The numbers here are illustrative.

title: Protein identification, abundance and structure
text: Distinguish peptide evidence, protein-group inference and abundance; evaluate missing values and transformations; interpret structural information without overclaiming function.

title: Protein identification, abundance and structure
text:
1. Biological question and measurements
Proteomics can quantify molecular evidence from peptides or proteins using platforms such as mass spectrometry. A measured peptide may be shared by multiple proteins; assigning it to a unique gene product is an inference problem. Identification confidence and abundance uncertainty are separate. Sample preparation, digestion, instrument response and batch effects influence measured values.
A protein table can contain missing values because abundance is low, a feature was not identified or processing failed. These mechanisms imply different analysis choices. Replacing every missing value by zero treats non-observation as a known measurement and can introduce artificial group differences. On a log scale, zero is not an absence: it represents an original-scale value of one.
Structural records describe coordinates of a measured or predicted molecular model. A geometrical contact suggests spatial proximity within that model; it does not alone establish biochemical interaction or functional importance.

title: Protein identification, abundance and structure
text:
2. Model and assumptions
If \(z=\log_2(x)\) for positive abundance x, a difference \(z_T-z_C\) corresponds to a ratio \(2^{z_T-z_C}\). The example compares arithmetic means of log2 measurements, so the ratio corresponds to geometric means on the original scale.
Complete-case comparisons require recording which values remain in each group. They can be biased when observation depends on abundance or group.

title: Protein identification, abundance and structure
text:
3. Worked example
The inputs below are hypothetical. Run the example, predict one change, then compare your prediction with the result. All executable code uses base R.


Show R code
z <- c(8,8.5,NA,9,9.2,NA)
group <- factor(c("C","C","C","T","T","T"))
means <- tapply(z,group,mean,na.rm=TRUE)
observed <- tapply(!is.na(z),group,sum)
data.frame(group=names(means),observed=as.vector(observed),mean_log2=as.vector(means))


  group observed mean_log2
1     C        2      8.25
2     T        2      9.10


Show R code
c(log2_difference=means["T"]-means["C"],
 geometric_mean_ratio=2^(means["T"]-means["C"]))


     log2_difference.T geometric_mean_ratio.T 
              0.850000               1.802501 


Both groups retain two measurements. The numerical ratio describes the observed log2 values, not a verified biological treatment effect.

title: Protein identification, abundance and structure
text:
4. Interpretation and scope
The teaching protein values are supplied log2 abundances. They are not raw spectra and do not implement peptide identification or protein inference. Report platform, processing, quantification scale, identification thresholds and missingness. Protein structure and abundance answer different questions.

What ratio corresponds to a log2 difference of one?
Why might low-value imputation strengthen a spurious difference?
Does a close residue pair establish an interaction in a living animal?







Suggested answers






Two.
If one group has more missing values, the imputation can manufacture a lower group mean; its assumptions need justification.
No; context, structural uncertainty and biological evidence are required.

title: Microbial communities and host relationships
text:
1. Biological question and measurements
A microbiome sample measures a community at a particular site, time and collection process. Amplicon data focus on selected marker sequences; shotgun metagenomics samples broader sequence content. Sequence representation depends on extraction, library preparation, genome properties and reference annotation. A taxonomic abundance profile does not directly measure metabolic activity.
Rumen, intestinal and faecal samples answer different questions. Host diet, genotype, management and physiology can influence the community while also influencing a production trait. Association between a taxon and methane, for example, can arise from those shared drivers; it does not demonstrate that changing the taxon would change emissions.

title: Microbial communities and host relationships
text:
2. Model and assumptions
Relative abundance is \(p_{ij}=x_{ij}/\sum_k x_{kj}\). Because the components sum to one, increasing one absolute component can reduce the relative representation of another whose absolute amount did not change.
For strictly positive components, a log ratio \(\log(x_A/x_B)\) is invariant to a common sample multiplier. Zero handling needs an explicit measurement assumption: adding an arbitrary constant can alter conclusions, especially for rare taxa.

title: Microbial communities and host relationships
text:
3. Worked example
The inputs below are hypothetical. Run the example, predict one change, then compare your prediction with the result. All executable code uses base R.


Show R code
absolute <- rbind(before=c(A=10,B=10,C=10),after=c(A=20,B=10,C=10))
relative <- absolute/rowSums(absolute)
relative


               A         B         C
before 0.3333333 0.3333333 0.3333333
after  0.5000000 0.2500000 0.2500000


Show R code
c(B_absolute_change=absolute[2,"B"]-absolute[1,"B"],
 B_relative_change=relative[2,"B"]-relative[1,"B"])


B_absolute_change B_relative_change 
       0.00000000       -0.08333333 


Show R code
stopifnot(absolute[2,"B"]==absolute[1,"B"],relative[2,"B"]<relative[1,"B"])
log(absolute[,"A"]/absolute[,"B"])


   before     after 
0.0000000 0.6931472 


B becomes a smaller fraction even though its absolute amount is unchanged. A change in total microbial load is not observable from these fractions alone.

title: Microbial communities and host relationships
text:
4. Interpretation and scope
Distinguish microbial load, relative composition, genetic potential and activity. Consider contaminants, reference coverage, repeated measurements, host-level confounding and independent validation. Host–microbiome co-metabolism is a mechanistic hypothesis to examine with appropriate molecular and experimental evidence.

Which taxon changed absolute amount?
Can relative B alone establish that B was depleted?
What extra measurement could inform total microbial load?







Suggested answers






A doubled.
No; its fraction decreased through the change in A.
A justified absolute-quantification measurement, such as calibrated load estimates, with its own sampling and technical assumptions.

title: Statistical models and honest validation

title: Statistical models and honest validation
text:
1. Biological question and measurements
High-dimensional assays contain correlated features, different scales and substantial measurement variation. More variables can improve a model, but can also overfit a small sample. Regression requires a stated response, experimental unit, design and assumptions. Clustering and principal components describe patterns; they do not prove biological mechanisms.
Inference estimates an effect and its uncertainty under a model. Prediction evaluates performance for the intended new population. A split between rows can be inadequate if records from the same animal, family, farm or time series appear in both sets. The validation group should represent the deployment task, and preprocessing must be fitted using training data only.

title: Statistical models and honest validation
text:
2. Model and assumptions
For standardised training features X and centred response y, ridge regression minimises \(\|y-X\beta\|^2+\lambda \|\beta\|^2\), giving \(\widehat\beta=(X^T X+\lambda I)^{-1}X^Ty\). A positive lambda shrinks coefficients; choose it using training-only validation, not test outcomes. The intercept is handled separately.
Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment addresses false-discovery-rate control under its applicable dependence conditions. An adjusted p-value is not the probability that an individual hypothesis is false.

title: Statistical models and honest validation
text:
3. Worked example
The inputs below are hypothetical. Run the example, predict one change, then compare your prediction with the result. All executable code uses base R.


Show R code
set.seed(1201)
X <- matrix(rnorm(30*4),30,4)
y <- 1+X[,1]-.5*X[,2]+rnorm(30)
train <- 1:20; test <- 21:30
center <- colMeans(X[train,]); scale_train <- apply(X[train,],2,sd)
Ztrain <- scale(X[train,],center,scale_train)
Ztest <- scale(X[test,],center,scale_train)
ybar <- mean(y[train]); lambda <- 2 # Supplied, not tuned on the test set.
beta <- solve(crossprod(Ztrain)+lambda*diag(4),crossprod(Ztrain,y[train]-ybar))
prediction <- as.vector(ybar+Ztest%*%beta)
c(test_RMSE=sqrt(mean((y[test]-prediction)^2)),
 baseline_RMSE=sqrt(mean((y[test]-ybar)^2)))


    test_RMSE baseline_RMSE 
     1.055431      1.539884 


Show R code
p.adjust(c(.001,.02,.04,.4),method="BH")


[1] 0.00400000 0.04000000 0.05333333 0.40000000


The test rows affect neither scaling nor coefficients. One split illustrates the process; its performance is not a stable estimate for a livestock population.

title: Statistical models and honest validation
text:
4. Interpretation and scope
Use appropriate loss and uncertainty, inspect residuals and state model-selection decisions. Screening features on all outcomes before splitting leaks information even if the final model is fitted on training rows. A penalty value selected on the test set turns it into a tuning set. The association practical distinguishes marker evidence from validated prediction.

title: Statistical models and honest validation
text:
5. Exercises

Why reuse training means for test scaling?
Can test RMSE be used to choose lambda and still be an untouched test score?
Does a PCA cluster establish a treatment effect?







Suggested answers






The deployment transformation must not depend on the new group’s distribution.
No; use a separate validation procedure within training, then evaluate once on test data.
No; batches, other covariates and sampling can also create clusters.

title: Pathway enrichment and biological networks
text: Define eligible backgrounds and selection rules; calculate enrichment under a supplied null; construct and interpret networks with explicit edge definitions.

title: Pathway enrichment and biological networks
text:
1. Biological question and measurements
A pathway analysis asks whether selected features are represented in a gene set more than expected under a specified model. Define the eligible background from genes that could have been selected, not every annotated gene regardless of assay coverage. Selection can depend on abundance, length, missingness or mapping, which can violate equal-selection assumptions.
A network represents entities as nodes and a defined relationship as edges. A correlation network, protein-interaction database and curated metabolic network have different edge meanings. A dense cluster can reflect a common driver, duplicated measurements or technical structure. Gene regulation involves direction and mechanism; undirected correlation alone supplies neither.

title: Pathway enrichment and biological networks
text:
2. Model and assumptions
With N eligible genes, K in a pathway and n selected genes, the hypergeometric null assumes a uniformly selected subset of size n. For overlap x, the enrichment tail is \(P(X\ge x)\) under \(X\sim Hypergeometric(N,K,n)\). If pathway tests are numerous, address multiplicity.
For a binary undirected adjacency matrix A with zero diagonal, degree is \(d_i=\sum_j A_{ij}\). It describes connectivity under the selected definition and threshold, not an intrinsic universal importance of the gene.

title: Pathway enrichment and biological networks
text:
3. Worked example
The inputs below are hypothetical. Run the example, predict one change, then compare your prediction with the result. All executable code uses base R.


Show R code
N <- 100; K <- 20; n <- 10; x <- 5
p <- phyper(x-1,K,N-K,n,lower.tail=FALSE)
c(expected_overlap=n*K/N,observed_overlap=x,enrichment_p=p)


expected_overlap observed_overlap     enrichment_p 
      2.00000000       5.00000000       0.02546455 


Show R code
A <- matrix(c(0,1,1,0,1,0,1,0,1,1,0,1,0,0,1,0),4,4,byrow=TRUE)
dimnames(A) <- list(paste0("g",1:4),paste0("g",1:4))
stopifnot(isSymmetric(A),all(diag(A)==0),sum(A)==2*4)
rowSums(A)


g1 g2 g3 g4 
 2  2  3  1 


The expected overlap is two under the supplied background and sampling rule. Degree depends on the four chosen nodes and their edges. These are fictional pathways and networks.

title: Pathway enrichment and biological networks
text:
4. Interpretation and scope
Overlapping gene sets and correlated gene statistics complicate enrichment inference. Report membership/version, mapping, background, selection rule and adjustment. Network robustness requires resampling or independent validation; causality requires stronger design or assumptions than correlation.

text:
5. Exercises

Why can a genome-wide background be inappropriate for a protein assay?
Does an enrichment p-value measure pathway activity?
What changes when a correlation threshold is raised?







Suggested answers






Many genes could not have been observed or selected.
No; it concerns representation under a null, not direct activity.
Edges and node degrees can change, showing their dependence on the supplied rule.

title: Single-cell, spatial and emerging methods

title: Single-cell, spatial and emerging methods
text:
1. Biological question and measurements
Single-cell assays can resolve molecular differences across sampled cells, but cells are nested within specimens and animals. Treatment allocation to an animal does not create independent treatment allocations to every sampled cell. Cell recovery and QC affect the representation of cell types. For an animal-level comparison, one approach aggregates measurements by animal and cell type before using an appropriate sample-level analysis; this still requires biological replication.
Spatial assays retain positional information at a platform-dependent resolution. Spots can mix cells, adjacent positions can be dependent, and resolution varies. Chromatin conformation assays estimate selected contact relationships, not a deterministic map of regulatory causation. Advanced epigenomic measurements retain their assay-specific limitations.
AI models can learn useful patterns, but a sophisticated architecture does not eliminate sample dependence, leakage or confounding. A generated explanation is not supporting biological evidence. Specify training data, evaluation units, uncertainty and validation context.

title: Single-cell, spatial and emerging methods
text:
2. Model and assumptions
For m cells per animal with equal marginal variance \(\sigma^2\) and within-animal correlation rho, a design-effect approximation is \(D=1+(m-1)\rho\). Treating \(nm\) cells as independent can overstate precision; \(nm/D\) is an effective-count illustration under this equal-correlation model, not a replacement for a valid hierarchical analysis or degrees of freedom.
For high-dimensional prediction, keep animals or specimens separated across training and evaluation when that represents the intended task.

text:
3. Worked example
The inputs below are hypothetical. Run the example, predict one change, then compare your prediction with the result. All executable code uses base R.


Show R code
animals <- 6; cells <- 100; rho <- .1
design_effect <- 1+(cells-1)*rho
c(raw_cell_count=animals*cells,
 equal_correlation_effective_count=animals*cells/design_effect,
 independent_animals=animals)


                   raw_cell_count equal_correlation_effective_count 
                        600.00000                          55.04587 
              independent_animals 
                          6.00000 


Show R code
set.seed(1601)
cell <- data.frame(animal=rep(paste0("a",1:6),each=10),
 value=rep(rnorm(6),each=10)+rnorm(60,sd=.2))
aggregate(value~animal,cell,mean)

3     a3 -1.1853579

4. Interpretation and scope
Evaluate cell-type annotation, recovery, doublets, QC, spatial scale and biological replication. Method-specific pipelines and validations are needed before a real analysis. Advanced extensions in this course critique supplied designs and evidence; they do not claim to implement single-cell or spatial software workflows.

title: Animal-production questions and integrated reporting
text: Translate a production question into design and analysis; evaluate usefulness at the intended decision time; communicate uncertainty, alternatives and follow-up.

title: Animal-production questions and integrated reporting
text:
1. Biological question and measurements
Animal-production applications include growth, feed efficiency, meat/milk quantity and quality, reproductive performance, health, environmental adaptation and methane. A molecular profile is useful only in relation to a defined question, decision, population and measurement cost. A statistically associated feature may add little predictive value; a predictor may work without identifying a causal mechanism.
An integrated study should specify the primary phenotype and units, experimental unit, target population, exposure, tissue/time, eligible assays, covariates, data processing, missingness and validation. Explain why each molecular layer is needed. A diet-intervention study and a breeding-value prediction study involve different causal and genetic objectives even if both record performance.

title: Animal-production questions and integrated reporting
text:
2. Model and assumptions
For a prediction comparison, calculate the same loss on the same held-out animals for a baseline and an augmented model. If errors are \(e_{i0}\) and \(e_{i1}\), the paired improvement in squared error is \(d_i=e_{i0}^2-e_{i1}^2\). Its mean is positive when the augmented model has smaller mean squared error in that group.
One evaluation set gives conditional evidence, not a universal benefit. Costs, feasibility, calibration, independent replication and relevance to selection or management still need assessment.

title: Animal-production questions and integrated reporting
text:
3. Worked example
The inputs below are hypothetical. Run the example, predict one change, then compare your prediction with the result. All executable code uses base R.


Show R code
observed <- c(10,12,9,14,11,13)
baseline <- c(11,11,11,11,11,11)
augmented <- c(10.5,11.7,9.5,13.4,11.2,12.7)
d <- (observed-baseline)^2-(observed-augmented)^2
c(baseline_RMSE=sqrt(mean((observed-baseline)^2)),
 augmented_RMSE=sqrt(mean((observed-augmented)^2)),
 paired_MSE_improvement=mean(d))


         baseline_RMSE         augmented_RMSE paired_MSE_improvement 
             1.7795130              0.4242641              2.9866667 


Show R code
stopifnot(abs(mean(d)-(mean((observed-baseline)^2)-mean((observed-augmented)^2)))<1e-12)


The supplied predictions improve squared-error loss for these six fictional animals. The calculation says nothing about how those predictions were trained or whether they generalize.

title: Animal-production questions and integrated reporting
text:
4. Interpretation and scope
Follow-up can include replication in a new farm, time, breed or management setting; a targeted assay or perturbation can address a mechanistic question. Choose follow-up to resolve the uncertainty actually present, not merely to generate more molecular measurements.

text:

Why compare predictions on the same test animals?
Does predictive improvement show that an assay measures a causal mediator?
What belongs in a concise final report?

It makes the comparison paired and avoids changing the population between models.
No; proxies can predict through correlation.

title: Basic sequence analysis and manipulation
text:
Biological question and data
How do file structure and unknown bases affect a sequence summary?
FASTA inputs contain only A, C, G, T and N; these teaching records have no quality scores. N is unknown and is excluded from the GC denominator.
No biological download is required. Numerical inputs are hypothetical, not observed animal data. The runnable examples use base R. Count and abundance units are specified where used.

title: Basic sequence analysis and manipulation
text:
1. Parse explicit records
Use the local teaching parser, which rejects missing headers, duplicate IDs and invalid bases.


Show R code
helper_dir <- if (dir.exists("R")) "R" else "../R"
stopifnot(file.exists(file.path(helper_dir,"sequence_helpers.R")))
source(file.path(helper_dir,"sequence_helpers.R"))
sequences <- read_teaching_fasta(c(">demo1","ACGTNN","GCGC",">demo2","TTTACG"))
sequences


       demo1        demo2 
"ACGTNNGCGC"     "TTTACG" 


Show R code
stopifnot(nchar(sequences["demo1"])==10)


Wrapped sequence lines are joined within their records. Sequence length includes unknown bases.

title: Basic sequence analysis and manipulation
text:
2. Calculate called-base summaries
Count unknowns separately. An all-unknown sequence has no estimable called-base GC proportion.


Show R code
summary_one <- function(s) {
 x <- strsplit(s,"")[[1]]; called <- x%in%c("A","C","G","T")
 c(length=length(x),called=sum(called),unknown=sum(!called),
 GC=if(any(called))mean(x[called]%in%c("G","C")) else NA_real_)
}
result <- t(vapply(sequences,summary_one,numeric(4)))
result


      length called unknown        GC
demo1     10      8       2 0.7500000
demo2      6      6       0 0.3333333


Show R code
stopifnot(abs(result["demo1","GC"]-6/8)<1e-12,
 is.na(summary_one("NNN")["GC"]))


demo1 has ten characters but eight called bases; six called bases are G or C.

title: Basic sequence analysis and manipulation
text:
3. Reverse-complement the sequence
Reverse the base order as well as complementing each symbol. Keep unknown N as N.


Show R code
reverse_complement <- function(s) {
 x <- rev(strsplit(s,"")[[1]])
 paste(unname(c(A="T",C="G",G="C",T="A",N="N")[x]),collapse="")
}
rc <- vapply(sequences,reverse_complement,character(1))
rc


       demo1        demo2 
"GCGCNNACGT"     "CGTAAA" 


Show R code
stopifnot(identical(unname(vapply(rc,reverse_complement,character(1))),unname(sequences)))


Reverse complementing twice restores the original sequence, a useful orientation check.

title: Basic sequence analysis and manipulation
text:
Interpretation and limits
Called-base GC is a descriptive proportion, not sequencing quality or coding potential. Unknown bases and selected regions can make whole-record comparisons misleading. This parser is intentionally small, not a general FASTA library.

title: Basic sequence analysis and manipulation
text:
Exercises

Recalculate GC including N in the denominator; explain the change.
Add a duplicate header.
Why does complementing without reversing give a different object?







Suggested answers






It decreases to 6/10, treating unknowns as if they were called non-GC bases.
The parser rejects the ambiguous identifier.
A reverse complement changes strand orientation; complement alone preserves the original character order.

title: Sequence similarity and evidence for homology
text:
Biological question and data
Does a high number of matching bases provide enough evidence to claim common ancestry or shared function?
Two supplied short sequences are compared at corresponding positions without gaps. A shuffle calculation conditions on one sequence’s base composition; it is a restricted teaching null, not BLAST or an evolutionary test.
No biological download is required. Numerical inputs are hypothetical, not observed animal data. The runnable examples use base R. Count and abundance units are specified where used.

title: Sequence similarity and evidence for homology
text:
1. Measure identity
The sequences have equal length. Record both matches and denominator.


Show R code
a <- strsplit("ACGTACGTACGTACGT","")[[1]]
b <- strsplit("ACGTACGTTCGTACGA","")[[1]]
stopifnot(length(a)==length(b))
observed <- sum(a==b)
c(matches=observed,length=length(a),identity=observed/length(a))


 matches   length identity 
  14.000   16.000    0.875 


Show R code
stopifnot(observed==14)


Fourteen of sixteen corresponding bases match in this supplied alignment.

title: Sequence similarity and evidence for homology
text:
2. Compare a restricted shuffle null
Shuffle the second sequence without changing composition. Include the usual plus-one Monte Carlo tail convention.


Show R code
set.seed(401)
shuffled <- replicate(499,sum(a==sample(b)))
p_mc <- (1+sum(shuffled>=observed))/(length(shuffled)+1)
c(shuffle_mean=mean(shuffled),observed=observed,shuffle_tail=p_mc)


shuffle_mean     observed shuffle_tail 
    4.084168    14.000000     0.002000 


Show R code
hist(shuffled,breaks=seq(-.5,16.5,1),xlab="Matches under composition shuffle",main="Restricted teaching null")
abline(v=observed,col="#d95f02",lwd=2)









This comparison shows what positional matches look like after a particular randomization. It ignores database size, local-alignment selection, substitution models and sequence dependence.

title: Sequence similarity and evidence for homology
text:
3. Separate claims
Place each claim beside the extra evidence it needs.


Show R code
claims <- data.frame(claim=c("sequence similarity","homology","shared function"),
 evidence=c("explicit aligned comparison","ancestry inference with appropriate context",
 "functional/domain/experimental evidence"))
claims


                claim                                    evidence
1 sequence similarity                 explicit aligned comparison
2            homology ancestry inference with appropriate context
3     shared function     functional/domain/experimental evidence


Homology is a relationship of common ancestry, not 87.5% homology. Shared function is a further biological claim.

title: Sequence similarity and evidence for homology
text:
Interpretation and limits
Use the NCBI BLAST glossary to distinguish identity and homology. The toy shuffle tail is not a database-search E-value and cannot be substituted for one.

title: Sequence similarity and evidence for homology
text:
Exercises

Compare two all-A sequences. Why is high identity weak evidence here?
What is ignored by positional comparison when lengths differ?
Does a small shuffle tail establish function?







Suggested answers






Low complexity makes agreement unsurprising; the composition-preserving shuffle gives the same matches.
Alignment, indels and local-versus-global coverage must be specified.
No; it addresses only the stated restricted null.

title: Distances, clustering and phylogenetic interpretation
text:
Biological question and data
What assumptions turn observed sequence differences into an evolutionary tree?
The supplied four-taxon distance matrix is fictional, additive and ultrametric. UPGMA is used only under this idealized equal-rate setting; it is not a general phylogenetic inference method.
No biological download is required. Numerical inputs are hypothetical, not observed animal data. The runnable examples use base R. Count and abundance units are specified where used.

title: Distances, clustering and phylogenetic interpretation
text:
1. Check the supplied distances
For the quartet ab|cd, the within-pair sum is smaller than the equal cross-pair sums.


Show R code
D <- matrix(c(0,2,6,6,2,0,6,6,6,6,0,2,6,6,2,0),4,4,byrow=TRUE,
 dimnames=list(c("a","b","c","d"),c("a","b","c","d")))
stopifnot(isSymmetric(D),all(diag(D)==0),all(D>=0))
sums <- c(ab_cd=D[1,2]+D[3,4],ac_bd=D[1,3]+D[2,4],ad_bc=D[1,4]+D[2,3])
sums


ab_cd ac_bd ad_bc 
    4    12    12 


Show R code
stopifnot(sums[2]==sums[3],sums[1]<sums[2])


The four-point relation supports the supplied split in an additive tree model. Exact equality is a feature of the constructed distances.

title: Distances, clustering and phylogenetic interpretation
text:
2. Build the idealized clustering tree
Average-linkage clustering is UPGMA. Tree branch heights can be interpreted with additional rate assumptions; plot heights are dissimilarities.


Show R code
fit <- hclust(as.dist(D),method="average")
plot(fit,ylab="Supplied dissimilarity",main="Idealized UPGMA example")









Show R code
reconstructed <- as.matrix(cophenetic(fit))
stopifnot(max(abs(reconstructed-D))<1e-12)
fit$height


[1] 2 2 6


The ideal matrix is exactly represented by the clustering ultrametric. That exact fit is not a general property of sequence distances.

title: Distances, clustering and phylogenetic interpretation
text:
3. Break the ideal assumption
Alter one pair symmetrically and measure the mismatch to its clustering representation.


Show R code
changed <- D; changed[1,3] <- changed[3,1] <- 8
other <- hclust(as.dist(changed),method="average")
c(max_cophenetic_discrepancy=max(abs(as.matrix(cophenetic(other))-changed)))


max_cophenetic_discrepancy 
                       1.5 


The new distances are no longer represented exactly by that UPGMA ultrametric.

title: Distances, clustering and phylogenetic interpretation
text:
Interpretation and limits
Real analyses must address sequence alignment, substitution model, rate differences, sampling and uncertainty. A gene tree can differ from population/species history through processes such as lineage sorting and recombination. Branches measured in substitutions cannot be labelled years without calibration.

title: Distances, clustering and phylogenetic interpretation
text:
Exercises

Why does UPGMA require an equal-rate interpretation for phylogeny?
Does exact reconstruction mean these fictional taxa exist?
What would a bootstrap assess?







Suggested answers






Its rooted ultrametric representation assumes equal root-to-tip evolutionary distances.
No; the matrix was constructed to illustrate the model.
Resampling stability conditional on the data and procedure, not proof that every evolutionary assumption holds.

title: Sequencing data quality assessment
text:
Biological question and data
How do low-quality positions influence a small read-quality summary?
The fictional FASTQ records use ASCII Phred+33 encoding. The error probabilities are interpreted as calibrated per-base probabilities solely for this example. The practical does not assess mapping or a real sequencing run.
No biological download is required. Numerical inputs are hypothetical, not observed animal data. The runnable examples use base R. Count and abundance units are specified where used.

title: Sequencing data quality assessment
text:
1. Decode quality strings
Confirm the sequence and quality strings have matching lengths.


Show R code
reads <- c(read1="ACGTACGT",read2="ACGTACGT",read3="ACGTNNGT")
quality <- c(read1="IIIIIIII",read2="IIII!!II",read3="55555555")
stopifnot(identical(names(reads),names(quality)),all(nchar(reads)==nchar(quality)))
Q <- t(vapply(quality,function(q) utf8ToInt(q)-33,numeric(8)))
Q


      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [,5] [,6] [,7] [,8]
read1   40   40   40   40   40   40   40   40
read2   40   40   40   40    0    0   40   40
read3   20   20   20   20   20   20   20   20


Show R code
stopifnot(Q[1,1]==40,Q[2,5]==0,Q[3,1]==20)


I encodes Q40, ! Q0 and 5 Q20 under the stated convention. The convention must not be guessed from appearance.

title: Sequencing data quality assessment
text:
2. Summarise errors and unknown calls
Sum encoded error probabilities and count unknown bases separately.


Show R code
expected_errors <- rowSums(10^(-Q/10))
unknown <- vapply(reads,function(s) sum(strsplit(s,"")[[1]]=="N"),integer(1))
qc <- data.frame(read=names(reads),mean_Q=rowMeans(Q),expected_errors,unknown)
qc


       read mean_Q expected_errors unknown
read1 read1     40          0.0008       0
read2 read2     30          2.0006       0
read3 read3     20          0.0800       2


Show R code
stopifnot(abs(expected_errors[1]-.0008)<1e-12,expected_errors[2]>2)


Two Q0 positions dominate the second read’s expected-error total. Mean quality alone compresses their location and severity.

title: Sequencing data quality assessment
section: 3. Apply and report a specified rule
text:
3. Apply and report a specified rule
The supplied rule retains reads with expected errors below .1 and no unknown calls; it is illustrative, not a universal threshold.


Show R code
qc$keep <- qc$expected_errors<.1 & qc$unknown==0
qc


       read mean_Q expected_errors unknown  keep
read1 read1     40          0.0008       0  TRUE
read2 read2     30          2.0006       0 FALSE
read3 read3     20          0.0800       2 FALSE


Show R code
c(input_reads=nrow(qc),retained=sum(qc$keep))


input_reads    retained 
          3           1 


Show R code
stopifnot(sum(qc$keep)==1)


The third read meets the encoded-error rule but fails the unknown-base rule. Report the exclusions and their reason.

title: Sequencing data quality assessment
text:
Interpretation and limits
Quality encoding, adapter content, length distributions, contaminants, mapping, coverage and sample identity matter in a complete sequencing workflow. A threshold chosen after looking at a desired result can bias downstream analysis. More retained reads do not create more biological replicates.

title: Sequencing data quality assessment
text:
Exercises

Why can mean Q hide a problematic read?
Does summing error probabilities require independent errors?
What information would mapping QC add?







Suggested answers






A few extremely low-quality positions can be diluted in the average.
No; expectation is additive. Independence matters for some probability calculations, not this sum.
Reference alignment, multimapping, coverage and mapping-rate patterns, each requiring interpretation.

title: Functional annotation and pathway enrichment

title: Functional annotation and pathway enrichment
text:
Biological question and data
Is a selected gene list enriched for a supplied pathway under an explicitly defined selection null?
The gene/pathway table is fictional. Every background gene is eligible, and the null treats a fixed-size selected set as uniformly drawn from that background. Selected genes are supplied for teaching, not discovered by a calibrated genome-wide analysis.
No biological download is required. Numerical inputs are hypothetical, not observed animal data. The runnable examples use base R. Count and abundance units are specified where used.

title: Functional annotation and pathway enrichment
text:
1. Define the eligible universe
Use the 24 assayed gene IDs and a prespecified six-gene list.


Show R code
helper_dir <- if (dir.exists("R")) "R" else "../R"
stopifnot(file.exists(file.path(helper_dir,"teaching_data.R")))
source(file.path(helper_dir,"teaching_data.R"))
d <- teaching_data()
background <- rownames(d$counts)
selected <- sprintf("gene%02d",1:6)
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(background),all(selected%in%background))
annotation <- d$annotation
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(annotation$gene),setequal(annotation$gene,background))
table(annotation$pathway)



pathwayA pathwayB pathwayC 
       8        8        8 


The measured universe is known. Counting annotations outside it would change the null population.

title: Functional annotation and pathway enrichment
text:
2. Calculate enrichment
For each set, compute overlap, null expectation and an upper-tail hypergeometric p-value. Confirm the first result with a 2-by-2 Fisher test.


Show R code
one_set <- function(pathway) {
 member <- annotation$gene[annotation$pathway==pathway]
 N <- length(background); K <- length(member); n <- length(selected)
 x <- sum(selected%in%member)
 c(N=N,K=K,n=n,x=x,expected=n*K/N,p=phyper(x-1,K,N-K,n,lower.tail=FALSE))
}
result <- as.data.frame(t(vapply(unique(annotation$pathway),one_set,numeric(6))))
result$BH <- p.adjust(result$p,"BH")
result


          N K n x expected          p           BH
pathwayA 24 8 6 6        2 0.00020803 0.0006240899
pathwayB 24 8 6 0        2 1.00000000 1.0000000000
pathwayC 24 8 6 0        2 1.00000000 1.0000000000


Show R code
z <- result[1,]
tab <- matrix(c(z$x,z$n-z$x,z$K-z$x,z$N-z$K-z$n+z$x),2,byrow=TRUE)
stopifnot(abs(fisher.test(tab,alternative="greater")$p.value-z$p)<1e-12)


PathwayA has six selected members in a background of eight pathway members. The enrichment model concerns gene-set representation, not measured pathway activity.

title: Functional annotation and pathway enrichment
section: 3. Change the background and explain the effect
text:
3. Change the background and explain the effect
Keep the pathway count fixed while adding unmeasured nonmembers to the universe. This is deliberately an inappropriate comparison for the same assay.


Show R code
data.frame(background=c("eligible panel","inflated universe"),
 N=c(24,100),p=c(phyper(5,8,16,6,lower.tail=FALSE),
 phyper(5,8,92,6,lower.tail=FALSE)))


         background   N           p
1    eligible panel  24 2.08030e-04
2 inflated universe 100 2.34889e-08


Adding many nonmembers makes the same overlap appear more surprising. That is a change in assumptions, not more biological evidence.

title: Functional annotation and pathway enrichment
text:
Interpretation and limits
Hypergeometric enrichment assumes an appropriate equal-selection null. Expression level, feature length, detectability, correlation and annotation overlap can require a more suitable method. Document mapping, set version, selection rule, background and multiplicity.

title: Functional annotation and pathway enrichment
text:
Exercises

Why exclude unmeasured genes from this universe?
Does a small p-value establish pathway activation?
What if one measured gene maps to three proteins?







Suggested answers






They could not have entered the selected list under this assay.
No; it is evidence about representation under the supplied null.
Define the gene/protein analysis unit and avoid counting repeated gene evidence as independent entries.

title: Biological data visualization with explicit units
text:
Biological question and data
Which plots reveal library-panel size, sample variation and possible confounding in a hypothetical experiment?
The shared fixture contains counts, log2 abundances and a response in arbitrary units. The plotted count-panel total includes only the 24 supplied features and is not a whole-library sequencing-depth estimate.
No biological download is required. Numerical inputs are hypothetical, not observed animal data. The runnable examples use base R. Count and abundance units are specified where used.

title: Biological data visualization with explicit units
section: 1. Inspect the design before the measurements
text:
1. Inspect the design before the measurements
Count independent animals within the crossed diet/batch design.


Show R code
helper_dir <- if (dir.exists("R")) "R" else "../R"
stopifnot(file.exists(file.path(helper_dir,"teaching_data.R")))
source(file.path(helper_dir,"teaching_data.R"))
d <- teaching_data()
meta <- d$metadata
xtabs(~diet+batch,meta)


            batch
diet          A  B
  control    12 12
  supplement 12 12


Show R code
barplot(xtabs(~diet+batch,meta),beside=TRUE,legend.text=TRUE,
 col=c("#86B7A3","#E5A66B"),ylab="Number of animals",xlab="Batch")









A balanced cross-tabulation addresses one aspect of design. It does not eliminate every source of confounding.

title: Biological data visualization with explicit units
text:
2. Compare count and abundance views
Use exposure-adjusted counts on a descriptive log2 scale for one gene, and already-log2 measurements for a protein.


Show R code
normalized <- sweep(d$counts,2,d$exposure,"/")
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
boxplot(log2(normalized[1,]+1)~meta$diet,xlab="Diet",ylab="log2 adjusted count + 1",
 main="gene01",col="#86B7A3")
boxplot(d$protein[1,]~meta$diet,xlab="Diet",ylab="Supplied log2 abundance",
 main="protein01",col="#E5A66B")









Show R code
par(mfrow=c(1,1))


The axes describe different measurement scales. The gene and protein labels are fictional and their plots do not establish a linked biological mechanism.

title: Biological data visualization with explicit units
section: 3. Show outcome distributions and paired measurements
text:
3. Show outcome distributions and paired measurements
Keep animal alignment explicit and label the outcome units.


Show R code
stopifnot(identical(colnames(d$protein),meta$animal))
plot(d$protein[1,],meta$response,col=as.integer(meta$diet),pch=19,
 xlab="protein01 log2 abundance",ylab="Response (arbitrary units)")
legend("topleft",levels(meta$diet),col=1:2,pch=19,bty="n")









Colour reveals whether pooled association might combine group shifts and within-group variation.

title: Biological data visualization with explicit units
text:
Interpretation and limits
Plots diagnose patterns; they do not replace a model or prove an effect. Avoid using different transformations without labelling them, selectively hiding outliers or interpreting one unusual point before checking its identity and processing.

title: Biological data visualization with explicit units
text:
Exercises

Why label the response as arbitrary units?
What could a pooled scatterplot hide?
Why is a plot of log2 counts not a differential-expression test?







Suggested answers






The fixture defines no physical calibration for the phenotype.
Different relationships within groups, batch shifts or unequal sampling.
It supplies neither the required model-based uncertainty nor multiplicity treatment.

title: Sample identity, table joins and missing assays
text:
Biological question and data
What happens when protein columns arrive in a different order from phenotype metadata?
Every fixture animal has an assay identifier. The shuffled column order is deliberate; the underlying biological labels remain correct. This checks metadata alignment, not physical sample identity.
No biological download is required. Numerical inputs are hypothetical, not observed animal data. The runnable examples use base R. Count and abundance units are specified where used.

title: Sample identity, table joins and missing assays
text:
1. Create a plausible order mismatch
Reverse the assay order while leaving labels attached. Dimensions still match.


Show R code
helper_dir <- if (dir.exists("R")) "R" else "../R"
stopifnot(file.exists(file.path(helper_dir,"teaching_data.R")))
source(file.path(helper_dir,"teaching_data.R"))
d <- teaching_data()
meta <- d$metadata
shuffled <- d$protein[,rev(seq_len(ncol(d$protein))),drop=FALSE]
stopifnot(ncol(shuffled)==nrow(meta),!identical(colnames(shuffled),meta$animal))
head(data.frame(metadata_animal=meta$animal,assay_column=colnames(shuffled)))


  metadata_animal assay_column
1        animal01     animal48
2        animal02     animal47
3        animal03     animal46
4        animal04     animal45
5        animal05     animal44
6        animal06     animal43


A dimension check alone cannot identify this mistake.

title: Sample identity, table joins and missing assays
text:
2. Align explicitly and verify identity
Require unique IDs and complete matches before reordering.


Show R code
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(meta$animal),!anyDuplicated(colnames(shuffled)))
idx <- match(meta$animal,colnames(shuffled))
stopifnot(!anyNA(idx))
aligned <- shuffled[,idx,drop=FALSE]
stopifnot(identical(colnames(aligned),meta$animal),
 max(abs(aligned-d$protein))<1e-12)
c(correct_cor=cor(aligned[1,],meta$response),
 wrong_order_cor=cor(shuffled[1,],meta$response))


    correct_cor wrong_order_cor 
      0.1567479      -0.1811823 


The correctly aligned table reproduces the original measurements exactly. A wrong-order association can disappear or change direction.

title: Sample identity, table joins and missing assays
section: 3. Separate missing animals from missing features
text:
3. Separate missing animals from missing features
Remove one entire assay column and compare this to NAs within otherwise present assays.


Show R code
partial <- aligned[,-1,drop=FALSE]
index <- match(meta$animal,colnames(partial))
c(animals_without_assay=sum(is.na(index)),
 missing_feature_values=sum(is.na(d$protein_missing)))


 animals_without_assay missing_feature_values 
                     1                     11 


Show R code
stopifnot(sum(is.na(index))==1,sum(is.na(d$protein_missing))==11)


An absent assay and an unobserved protein value need different handling and reporting. Neither is a measured zero.

title: Sample identity, table joins and missing assays
text:
Interpretation and limits
ID matching preserves supplied labels but cannot detect a mislabeled specimen collected in the field. Use collection records and appropriate sample-identity checks for real data. Avoid silent complete-case deletion when missing assays relate to treatment or health.

title: Sample identity, table joins and missing assays
text:
Exercises

Why does a sorted join still need an identity check?
What if one metadata animal has two assay columns?
Why is a missing protein value not log2 zero?







Suggested answers






Sorting conventions and keys can differ between tables.
Define technical replicates or repeated specimens explicitly; do not choose a duplicate silently.
Missing means unobserved; log2 zero corresponds to an original-scale value of one.

title: Quality assessment and preprocessing across omics layers
text:
Biological question and data
Can the same quality rule and transformation be applied indiscriminately to counts, protein abundances and metabolites?
Counts are nonnegative integer measurements; protein and metabolite matrices are supplied log2 abundances. Missing proteins are deliberately inserted. All samples are fictional animals with explicit metadata.
No biological download is required. Numerical inputs are hypothetical, not observed animal data. The runnable examples use base R. Count and abundance units are specified where used.

title: Quality assessment and preprocessing across omics layers
text:
1. Audit each assay separately
Check IDs, dimensions, missingness and the supplied measurement scale.


Show R code
helper_dir <- if (dir.exists("R")) "R" else "../R"
stopifnot(file.exists(file.path(helper_dir,"teaching_data.R")))
source(file.path(helper_dir,"teaching_data.R"))
d <- teaching_data()
assays <- list(counts=d$counts,protein=d$protein_missing,metabolite=d$metabolite)
audit <- do.call(rbind,lapply(names(assays),function(name) {

 stopifnot(identical(colnames(X),d$metadata$animal))

How does treating a missing protein measurement as zero change a group comparison?
The supplied values are fictional log2 protein abundances, not raw peptide spectra. Missingness was inserted into the fixture. The contrast is descriptive and does not implement peptide identification, protein inference or a calibrated differential-abundance pipeline.

2. Fit ridge with a separate unpenalized intercept
Use the minimization convention sum of squared errors plus lambda times squared coefficient norm.

 crossprod(Z[train,,drop=FALSE],y[train]-ybar))

 crossprod(Z[train,,drop=FALSE],y[train]-ybar)))
stopifnot(normal_equation_error<1e-9)


The penalty shrinks standardized feature coefficients. Its magnitude depends on the stated objective scaling; software conventions can differ.

Feature selection, scaling, imputation and lambda tuning must occur inside training-only validation. If lambda is optimized on these test animals, they become a tuning set. For real prediction, use a grouping/time split matching deployment and quantify uncertainty across independent units.

How stable is a correlation edge when a small set of fictional animals is resampled?

title: Epigenomic coverage and cell-composition effects
text:
Biological question and data
Can a bulk-tissue methylation difference arise with no within-cell-type regulatory change?
Two fictional cell types have constant methylation probabilities .2 and .8. Group-specific cell mixture determines the pooled probability. Reads are binomial conditional on that probability; this simplified model does not represent all assay or biological variation.
No biological download is required. Numerical inputs are hypothetical, not observed animal data. The runnable examples use base R. Count and abundance units are specified where used.

title: Transcriptomics and expression analysis
text:
1. Start with the biological comparison
Imagine a feeding experiment asking whether a supplement changes transcription in liver tissue. The question must identify the animals, tissue, collection time and comparison. A sample collected after a meal may answer a different question from a fasting sample. Differences between tissues can be much larger than the treatment effect of interest.
Bulk RNA-seq pools RNA from the cells present in a sample. Higher abundance of an immune-cell transcript could reflect more immune cells, more transcription per immune cell, or both. Even an accurately estimated tissue-level difference does not distinguish these explanations by itself. RNA abundance also need not predict protein abundance: translation, degradation and collection timing intervene between the two measurements.
The experimental unit follows treatment allocation. If diet is independently assigned to animals, animals provide biological replication. If diet is assigned to pens, animals within a pen share the treatment unit; treating all animals as independent treatment replicates can exaggerate precision. More sequencing reads improve measurement of a library, but do not create additional animals or pens. Repeated tissues from one animal require their dependence to be considered.






Define the target before analysing



Write a sentence such as: “Compare liver transcript abundance between supplemented and control animals at the specified collection time, accounting for processing batch.” Then ask whether the allocation, sampling and metadata support that sentence.

title: Transcriptomics and expression analysis
text:
2. From tissue to count matrix
The measurement passes through several stages. At each stage, retain the information needed to explain the resulting counts.








Stage
What happens
What can change interpretation?




Sampling
Tissue is collected and stored
Time, tissue region, cell mixture, RNA degradation


Library preparation
RNA is selected and converted into a sequencing library
Selection protocol, strandedness, preparation batch


Sequencing
Fragments are represented by sequence reads
Depth, base quality, contamination


Alignment or quantification
Reads are related to a reference
Reference assembly, annotation version, ambiguous mapping


Feature summarization
Evidence is assigned to genes or transcripts
Counting rules, overlapping features, transcript aggregation


Statistical analysis
Replicated samples are compared
Design, normalization, dispersion and contrast



For paired-end data, the two reads usually describe the ends of one fragment. The counting convention should make clear whether the output counts fragments or reads. Gene-level summarization combines evidence from transcripts, so a change in isoform usage may be obscured by an unchanged total gene count. A count matrix is therefore already a processed measurement, not a direct census of RNA molecules.
Rows should have stable feature identifiers and columns should have unique sample identifiers. Match sample names explicitly to metadata. Keep the reference and annotation versions: changing annotation can alter which reads are assigned to a gene even if the biological samples are unchanged.

title: Transcriptomics and expression analysis
section: 3. Depth and composition are different problems
text:
3. Depth and composition are different problems

Known exposure
A convenient teaching model is that expected count equals exposure times abundance:
\[\mu_{gj}=s_j q_{gj}.\]
Here \(g\) indexes genes, \(j\) indexes samples, \(s_j\) describes relative exposure and \(q_{gj}\) is the expected count at unit exposure. If exposure doubles while abundance is unchanged, expected count doubles. Dividing counts by known exposure gives a useful descriptive comparison, although the counts still have sampling variation.
The following hypothetical calculation isolates this relationship:


Show R code
counts <- c(80,120,160)
exposure <- c(.8,1.2,1.6)
data.frame(counts,exposure,adjusted=counts/exposure)


  counts exposure adjusted
1     80      0.8      100
2    120      1.2      100
3    160      1.6      100


Show R code
stopifnot(all(counts/exposure==100))




Composition
Actual libraries are sampled from a mixture of transcripts. If a few transcripts occupy much more of a library, other transcripts can receive a smaller fraction of reads even when their abundance per cell is unchanged. Scaling by the total count cannot establish an absolute abundance scale.


Show R code
# Hypothetical molecule abundances; only gene A changes.
molecules <- cbind(control=c(A=100,B=100,C=100),
                  supplement=c(A=400,B=100,C=100))
fractions <- sweep(molecules,2,colSums(molecules),"/")
expected_counts <- 600*fractions
round(expected_counts,1)


  control supplement
A     200        400
B     200        100
C     200        100


Show R code
data.frame(gene=rownames(molecules),
 true_ratio=molecules[,2]/molecules[,1],
 observed_fraction_ratio=fractions[,2]/fractions[,1])


  gene true_ratio observed_fraction_ratio
A    A          4                     2.0
B    B          1                     0.5
C    C          1                     0.5


Show R code
stopifnot(molecules["B",2]==molecules["B",1],
          fractions["B",2]<fractions["B",1])


Gene B appears reduced on the fraction scale despite unchanged molecule abundance. This deliberately extreme example shows why the normalization reference matters. Methods based on a set of relatively stable genes require assumptions about that reference. External controls can help address some questions, but their interpretation depends on when and how they were added. A control added per mass of extracted RNA does not automatically provide RNA abundance per cell.


Choose the scale for the question








Quantity
Useful question
Main limitation




Raw counts
How much evidence was assigned to a feature?
Exposure differs between samples


CPM
What share of counted evidence belongs to a feature?
Sensitive to library composition


TPM
How is length-adjusted abundance distributed within a sample?
Relative scale; not direct input to a standard raw-count model


Normalized counts
How does a gene compare across samples under a normalization reference?
Depends on the normalization assumptions


Transformed expression
How do samples or expression patterns relate descriptively?
Transformation is not itself a differential-expression test



Gene length matters when comparing different genes’ abundance. For the same gene across samples, a fixed length alone does not explain a treatment difference. Transcript usage and sample-specific effective length can complicate that simplification.

title: Transcriptomics and expression analysis
text:
4. Count models and biological variation
A Poisson model assumes variance equals the mean. Independent biological samples often vary more than that. A negative-binomial model allows:
\[K_{gj}\sim NB(\mu_{gj},\alpha_g),\qquad
\mathrm{Var}(K_{gj})=\mu_{gj}+\alpha_g \mu_{gj}^2.\]
The dispersion \(\alpha_g\) controls the additional variation. Under this parameterization, the squared coefficient of variation is \(1/\mu+\alpha\). At high abundance, additional reads reduce the first term, while the dispersion term remains. This explains why sequencing deeper cannot substitute indefinitely for biological replication.


Show R code
mu <- c(10,100,1000)
alpha <- .1
data.frame(mean=mu,Poisson_variance=mu,
 NB_variance=mu+alpha*mu^2,NB_CV=sqrt(1/mu+alpha))


  mean Poisson_variance NB_variance     NB_CV
1   10               10          20 0.4472136
2  100              100        1100 0.3316625
3 1000             1000      101000 0.3178050


Show R code
curve(sqrt(1/x+alpha),from=1,to=1000,log="x",
 xlab="Expected count",ylab="Coefficient of variation",
 main="Hypothetical negative-binomial variation")
abline(h=sqrt(alpha),lty=2,col="#A65334")









Dispersion estimation is especially difficult with few samples. RNA-seq methods can share information across features to stabilize estimation. An unusually variable gene still requires scrutiny; sharing information is not a reason to ignore sample quality or experimental design.
The base-R practical uses quasi-Poisson regression with \(\mathrm{Var}(K)=\phi_g \mu\). That lets us inspect the mean model and estimated uncertainty with minimal dependencies, but its variance function differs from the negative-binomial generator. It supplies an approximate teaching analysis, whose calibration is not established by a successful fit.

title: Transcriptomics and expression analysis
text:
5. Design, offsets and contrasts
For a binary treatment and batch indicator, consider:
\[\log(\mu_{gj})=\log(s_j)+\beta_{0g}
+\beta_{Dg}D_j+\beta_{Bg}B_j.\]
An offset is a predictor whose coefficient is fixed to one: the model uses the supplied exposure rather than estimating an exposure effect. With control as the treatment reference, \(\beta_{Dg}\) compares supplement with control at the same batch. The abundance ratio is \(\exp(\beta_{Dg})\) and the log2 fold change is \(\beta_{Dg}/\log(2)\). A log2 fold change of 1 means a doubling; -1 means a halving.
Batch adjustment and normalization serve different purposes. Normalization addresses a measurement scale. Including batch describes systematic differences associated with a recorded processing factor. Normalized counts can still show batch structure, and adding batch cannot rescue an unidentified treatment comparison.
If all control samples are processed in batch A and all supplemented samples in batch B, treatment and batch columns convey the same information. The data cannot separate their effects. More reads from those same samples do not change that fact. Crossed allocation, with both diets represented in each batch, provides the within-batch comparisons needed for separation.
An additive model assumes the diet ratio is the same across batches. An interaction permits it to differ, changing what each coefficient means and increasing the information required. Covariates also need a biological rationale: adjusting for a variable affected by treatment can change the target from the overall treatment effect to a conditional comparison.

title: Transcriptomics and expression analysis
text:
6. Explore samples before interpreting tests
Inspect sample identifiers, metadata, count distributions and quality records together. A sample with a small total could reflect shallow sequencing or a failed preparation. A distribution alone seldom identifies the cause. For a small selected panel, its column sum is only a panel total, not a whole-library depth measure.
PCA summarizes dominant variation in a transformed expression matrix. Colour samples by treatment and use a second visual encoding for batch. Separation by treatment is compatible with a treatment response, but also with confounding. An isolated point is a prompt to inspect records, not automatic permission to delete the animal.
PCA depends on the transformation and scaling. Scaling every gene to unit variance gives low-variance genes more influence than an unscaled analysis. A plot of 24 teaching genes cannot represent the full complexity of a transcriptome. For real data, select the transformation and feature set deliberately and document them.

title: Transcriptomics and expression analysis
text:
7. Effects, uncertainty and multiple testing
An estimated effect answers how large the fitted comparison is. Its standard error describes uncertainty under the model. A confidence interval makes that uncertainty visible; a small p-value alone does not tell us whether the difference matters for production or health.
Testing many genes creates opportunities for false discoveries. Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment targets false discovery rate under its applicable assumptions. An adjusted p-value is not the probability that a particular gene’s null hypothesis is true. An FDR threshold also does not guarantee an exact false-discovery proportion in one dataset.
Feature filtering should be specified without selecting genes because they support the desired result. Low-information filtering and independent filtering used by RNA-seq methods require consideration of their relationship to the test statistic under the null. Report the tested feature universe, particularly before pathway analysis.
Use an effect-size plot alongside a results table. A large uncertain estimate deserves a different description from a modest precisely estimated effect. Pointwise 95% intervals shown for many genes are not simultaneous 95% coverage intervals. Shrinkage can stabilize noisy effect estimates for ranking and display, but must be labelled so readers understand which estimator is reported.

title: Transcriptomics and expression analysis
section: 8. From a teaching model to a full workflow
text:
8. From a teaching model to a full workflow
The practical exposes the calculations using hypothetical counts. A real analysis additionally needs assay quality records, a documented reference, appropriate count import, justified normalization, dispersion estimation, diagnostics and a specified contrast. The DESeq2 vignette is the technical reference for its negative-binomial implementation.
The natural follow-on practical would use a small, openly available real count matrix with documented biological replication and a tested Bioconductor environment. It should ask students to compare an exploratory impression with a fitted contrast, investigate a diagnostic concern and write a biological conclusion. Real gene names would allow pathway interpretation, while the sampling design would determine what claims are supported.

X_bad <- model.matrix(~diet+batch,confounded)

 columns=c(ncol(X),ncol(X_bad)),rank=c(qr(X)$rank,qr(X_bad)$rank))

title: RNA-seq counts, contrasts and uncertainty
section: 5. Explore samples on a descriptive scale
text:
5. Explore samples on a descriptive scale
PCA uses animals as observations and genes as variables. Here we use log2 exposure-adjusted counts with a pseudocount of one and centre each gene without scaling it to unit variance. This is a teaching transformation rather than a fitted variance-stabilizing transformation.


Show R code
log_expression <- log2(normalized+1)
pc <- prcomp(t(log_expression),center=TRUE,scale.=FALSE)
percent <- 100*pc$sdev^2/sum(pc$sdev^2)
diet_colour <- c(control="#267A67",supplement="#B85E32")
batch_shape <- c(A=16,B=17)
plot(pc$x[,1:2],col=diet_colour[as.character(meta$diet)],
 pch=batch_shape[as.character(meta$batch)],
 xlab=sprintf("PC1 (%.1f%%)",percent[1]),
 ylab=sprintf("PC2 (%.1f%%)",percent[2]))
legend("topright",legend=names(diet_colour),col=diet_colour,pch=16,bty="n")
legend("bottomright",legend=paste("Batch",names(batch_shape)),
 pch=batch_shape,bty="n")









Describe what you see before inspecting p-values. Do the diets overlap? Does batch appear related to either axis? Neither clustering nor separation provides a test of the fitted diet contrast. Known exposure adjustment does not remove the simulated batch effect.

title: RNA-seq counts, contrasts and uncertainty
text:
6. Inspect a fitted gene
Fit gene01 again and examine its fitted means and Pearson residuals. A residual is a discrepancy between an observation and its fitted expectation. We plot residuals rather than silently excluding an unusual animal.


Show R code
gene1 <- glm(counts["gene01",]~diet+batch+offset(log(exposure)),
             data=meta,family=quasipoisson())
fit_mean <- fitted(gene1)
pearson <- residuals(gene1,type="pearson")
plot(fit_mean,pearson,col=diet_colour[as.character(meta$diet)],
 pch=16,xlab="Fitted expected count",ylab="Pearson residual")
abline(h=0,lty=2)









Show R code
ord <- order(abs(pearson),decreasing=TRUE)
head(data.frame(animal=meta$animal[ord],observed=counts["gene01",ord],
 fitted=fit_mean[ord],residual=pearson[ord]),4)

animal26 animal26      170  90.31419 8.384998
animal36 animal36      263 160.93581 8.045389
animal40 animal40      254 160.93581 7.335949
animal14 animal14      146  90.31419 5.859580


Show R code

Look for systematic changes in residual spread or isolated discrepancies. The quasi-Poisson variance is proportional to the mean, while the generator also contains a squared-mean term. A visually acceptable plot does not establish correct p-value calibration. Gene01 additionally has an omitted genotype effect; the model should be assessed against the biological question rather than only the plot.
For comparison, fit a Poisson model to the same mean structure. Its standard error assumes less biological variation. Both fits use the same observations and mean model, so this comparison isolates the variance assumption.


Show R code
poisson1 <- update(gene1,family=poisson())
se_comparison <- c(Poisson=coef(summary(poisson1))["dietsupplement","Std. Error"],
 Quasi_Poisson=coef(summary(gene1))["dietsupplement","Std. Error"])/log(2)

text:
7. Report effects alongside uncertainty
