title: RNA-seq counts, contrasts and uncertainty
text:
8. Write the analysis record
For your report, state the experimental unit, sample numbers, tested features, supplied exposure, design formula, contrast direction, variance model and multiplicity procedure. Report one effect with its interval and distinguish the fitted tissue-level comparison from a mechanism claim. Record sessionInfo() when reproducing the practical.
A full real-data extension should retain this reporting discipline while replacing the simplified analysis with an appropriate documented RNA-seq workflow. Keep raw-count input, descriptive transformations and normalized displays conceptually separate.

title: RNA-seq counts, contrasts and uncertainty
text:
Further reading
The Harvard Introduction to Differential Gene Expression Analysis offers a complementary teaching sequence. The calculations and figures here are original hypothetical examples. Consult the DESeq2 vignette when moving to its implementation.

title: Biological questions and omics measurements
section: Define what an omics layer contributes
text:
Define what an omics layer contributes
An omics layer is a measurement system with a biological target and an observation process. Genomic dosage describes inherited alleles at measured sites. RNA, proteins and metabolites reflect tissue, time and physiological state. A microbial profile concerns organisms and their genetic potential or activity; a phenotype describes the animal or production system. These layers overlap in biological meaning but have different errors and units.
Consider a proposed chain from genotype to RNA to protein to a production phenotype. Each arrow asks a distinct question. Does a variant alter a transcript in this tissue? Does that transcript change a protein under these conditions? Does the protein affect the phenotype, or merely accompany it? Feedback can run in the other direction: disease or diet can change molecular profiles. A cross-sectional chain of correlations does not establish that ordered process.









Purpose
Target
Useful evidence
Main danger




Description
What differs between sampled groups?
Defined samples and measurement scale
Treating a selected sample as the whole population


Association
Which measurements vary together?
Replication and adjustment with a rationale
Shared causes or reverse direction


Prediction
What will happen for new animals?
Information available at decision time and independent evaluation
Leakage or a changed deployment population


Intervention
What would change under an action?
Allocation or justified causal assumptions
Confounding and an ill-defined action


Mechanism
Through what process does change occur?
Temporal and perturbation evidence
Treating a correlated molecular feature as a mediator

title: Biological questions and omics measurements
text:
Measurement error and biological signal
A useful introductory decomposition is \(X=S+E\), with biological signal \(S\) and measurement error \(E\). If the terms are independent, observed variance is the sum of their variances. More variability in a feature need not mean more biological information. A noisy assay can appear striking in an unscaled plot and still be an unreliable predictor.
In a hypothetical classical-error example, adding independent noise to a predictor attenuates its expected simple regression slope. This statement requires the independent-error model; systematic batch error can have a different effect.


Show R code
set.seed(101)
signal <- rnorm(2000)
response <- 2*signal+rnorm(2000)
noisy <- signal+rnorm(2000,sd=2)
c(clean_slope=coef(lm(response~signal))[2],
 noisy_slope=coef(lm(response~noisy))[2],
 expected_noisy_slope=2/(1+4))


  clean_slope.signal    noisy_slope.noisy expected_noisy_slope 
           2.0177279            0.4004118            0.4000000 


The observed noisy slope need not equal the expectation exactly. Recovering the biological slope requires information about measurement reliability and a suitable model; simply increasing the number of noisy columns is not a correction.

title: Biological questions and omics measurements
text:
Build a study argument
Begin with a target population and a decision: predicting later growth in a specified breed is different from explaining a diet response in a sampled group. State the outcome and its units, the allocation unit, measurement times and what contrast will be reported. For each assay, write the extra question it answers. If two layers provide the same information for the current decision, their acquisition cost and failure rate still matter.
Check feasibility before collecting data. A day-14 blood assay may be practical for monitoring but unavailable for a day-1 management decision. A liver measurement may address mechanism while being unsuitable for routine selection. Separate scientific usefulness from deployment usefulness.






Discussion: choose the evidence





A protein predicts methane output, and the protein is associated with diet. What experiment would test whether changing the protein changes methane? A perturbation directed at the proposed mechanism, with appropriate controls and outcomes, addresses a different question from another observational association study. Changing diet alone may alter many pathways, so it need not isolate that protein’s role.

title: Biological questions and omics measurements
text:
Further reading
EMBL-EBI introductory bioinformatics introduces the major resources. For a broader integration perspective, see Integrative omics for health and disease, Nature Reviews Genetics. Ask which ideas transfer to animal production and which depend on the original clinical setting.

title: Experimental design and biological sampling
section: Plan allocation, sampling and processing separately
text:
Plan allocation, sampling and processing separately
Random allocation concerns the biological intervention. Randomized processing order concerns how samples encounter technical conditions. These operations protect different comparisons. A biologically randomized study can still have diet perfectly confounded with extraction day; randomizing extraction alone does not make an observational exposure a randomized intervention.
Blocking forms comparisons within a known source of variation, such as farm or baseline weight class. For a balanced two-diet study, both diets should occur within the relevant block where feasible. Record the actual allocation, not just the intended schedule. Blinding helps prevent group knowledge from influencing handling or interpretation; it does not remove differences already present in a design.
A sample sheet should connect subject, biological specimen and assay aliquot. Keep repeated times explicit. The same animal can supply several samples, and one specimen can supply several technical preparations. A missing assay is not the same as an animal excluded from the whole experiment.

title: Experimental design and biological sampling
text:
Replication, dependence and effective information
For equal clusters with \(m\) animals per pen and within-pen correlation \(\rho\), the variance inflation for a simple average relative to independent animals is \(D=1+(m-1)\rho\). This is an illustrative equal-correlation model, not a substitute for specifying the treatment unit and fitting an appropriate analysis.


Show R code
m <- c(1,5,10,20)
rho <- .2
data.frame(animals_per_pen=m,design_effect=1+(m-1)*rho,
 information_relative_to_independence=1/(1+(m-1)*rho))


  animals_per_pen design_effect information_relative_to_independence
1               1           1.0                            1.0000000
2               5           1.8                            0.5555556
3              10           2.8                            0.3571429
4              20           4.8                            0.2083333


When diet is assigned to pens, precision of its comparison depends strongly on the number of independent pens. More animals per pen can improve measurement of a pen response but cannot create new treatment allocations. The same reasoning explains why technical duplicate libraries cannot replace missing biological replicates.

title: Experimental design and biological sampling
section: Balance and precision are different checks
text:
Balance and precision are different checks
A full-rank design can be highly unbalanced. Sparse cells create uncertain comparisons even when a coefficient exists. Inspect counts within treatment-by-batch combinations, then ask whether the target contrast relies on a small subgroup.


Show R code
layout <- data.frame(group=factor(rep(c('C','T'),c(9,3))),
 batch=factor(c(rep('A',5),rep('B',4),'A','B','B')))
xtabs(~group+batch,layout)


     batch
group A B
    C 5 4
    T 1 2


Show R code
X <- model.matrix(~group+batch,layout)
stopifnot(qr(X)$rank==ncol(X))
# With independent residual variance one, diagonal entries describe
# coefficient variances under this particular fixed design.
diag(solve(crossprod(X)))


(Intercept)      groupT      batchB 
  0.1794872   0.4615385   0.3461538 


This calculation conditions on the supplied linear model and residual variance. It shows where design information enters uncertainty, without providing a universal recommended sample count.

title: Experimental design and biological sampling
section: Specify exclusions and missingness before seeing effects
text:
Specify exclusions and missingness before seeing effects
An independently justified failed-assay rule is different from removing a sample because it weakens the desired contrast. Record the reason, when it was identified, affected assays and sensitivity of conclusions. If treatment changes survival or sample availability, the remaining observations may represent a selected subset rather than the original population.
Power planning needs a biologically meaningful effect, relevant variability, allocation structure, assay reliability and a multiplicity strategy. Sensitivity calculations across plausible inputs are more informative than a single optimistic number. Pilot variance estimates can themselves be uncertain. A design decision should also consider animal welfare, collection burden and feasible independent replication.






Design challenge





Two farms each receive only one diet. Is farm adjustment sufficient? No: there is no within-farm treatment comparison. If each farm instead has independently allocated pens receiving both diets, the design supplies comparisons, although pen dependence and the small number of farms still matter for generalization.

title: Experimental design and biological sampling
text:
Further reading
Use the NC3Rs experimental-unit guidance alongside the design practical. Compare its allocation examples with your own animal, pen and repeated-sampling hierarchy.

title: Biological databases and identifier mapping
section: Separate records, evidence and biological entities
text:
Separate records, evidence and biological entities
A sequence archive stores submitted measurement records; a reference resource organizes a selected assembly and annotation; a curated protein resource combines sequence with evaluated evidence. These are complementary roles. A cross-reference links records, but does not imply that all linked claims have the same evidence or review status.
Before querying, state the entity: a study, specimen, gene, transcript, protein product, sequence region or pathway. A gene symbol is convenient for display; an accession and version are usually better for traceable retrieval. Keep the original identifiers even after adding readable labels. Distinguish missing annotation from a measured absence of the molecule.








Mapping
Why several records arise
Analysis consequence




Gene to transcript
Alternative transcript models
One gene effect can appear in several annotation rows


Peptide to protein
Shared sequence
Protein identity may be ambiguous


Feature to metabolite
Candidate chemical assignments
Pathway membership may remain uncertain


Gene to orthologue
Duplication and evolutionary history
Cross-species transfer can be one-to-many

title: Biological databases and identifier mapping
section: Coordinates are part of the identifier
text:
Coordinates are part of the identifier
A position is incomplete without chromosome, assembly and convention. One-based closed intervals include both endpoints; zero-based half-open intervals include the start and exclude the end. Thus a one-based interval 101–110 and a zero-based half-open interval 100–110 can describe the same ten bases.


Show R code
closed_start <- 101L;closed_end <- 110L
half_open_start <- closed_start-1L;half_open_end <- closed_end
c(closed_length=closed_end-closed_start+1L,
 half_open_length=half_open_end-half_open_start)


   closed_length half_open_length 
              10               10 


Show R code
stopifnot(closed_end-closed_start+1L==half_open_end-half_open_start)


The arithmetic is simple, but an unnoticed convention mismatch can shift overlap calculations. Conversion of convention is also different from transferring coordinates between assemblies. Assembly transfer requires a mapping and can leave regions unmatched or ambiguous.

title: Biological databases and identifier mapping
section: Audit a mapping before using it
text:
Audit a mapping before using it
Report input keys, unique matched keys, unmatched keys and row expansion. Count unique biological entities for questions about entity overlap; count annotation rows only when rows are the intended unit. Avoid silently taking the first transcript returned by a database as the biologically relevant transcript.


Show R code
input <- data.frame(feature=c('f1','f2','f3','f4'))
map <- data.frame(feature=c('f1','f1','f2','f4'),
 gene=c('gA','gB','gB','gC'))
audit <- merge(input,map,all.x=TRUE)
data.frame(input_features=nrow(input),annotation_rows=nrow(audit),
 matched_features=length(unique(audit$feature[!is.na(audit$gene)])),
 distinct_genes=length(unique(na.omit(audit$gene))))


  input_features annotation_rows matched_features distinct_genes
1              4               5                3              3


The same gB is linked to two features, while f1 links to two genes. Deduplication cannot be solved by a universal rule: aggregation changes the measurement represented. Document the choice before enrichment or integration.

title: Biological databases and identifier mapping
text:
Search, retrieve and assess
For a public-study exercise, first read the experiment description and sample metadata. A downloadable expression matrix can lack the variables needed for the intended comparison. Check species, tissue, group definitions, biological replication and processing before considering its size.
Preserve the retrieval query, file checksum, reference versions and a local processing record. A later database update may improve annotation while changing results; reproducibility and current interpretation can require both the original mapping and a documented update.






Record-review challenge





A protein record cites experimental evidence for an enzymatic function in one species. What justifies assigning that function to a livestock gene? Evaluate the evolutionary relationship, sequence/domain evidence and experimental context. A cross-reference or similar name alone does not establish identical function.

title: Biological databases and identifier mapping
text:
Further reading
The EMBL-EBI introductory pathway links gene, protein and structure resources. NCBI GEO record documentation explains its record hierarchy; use it to distinguish a sample record from a study series.

title: Programming and reproducible data handling
section: Data objects should express the scientific unit
text:
Data objects should express the scientific unit
A matrix has dimensions and values, but the scientific meaning comes from labels and units. A long table with one row per animal–time–feature observation differs from metadata with one row per animal. State the key for every table. If several rows share an animal ID legitimately, joining on animal alone can multiply measurements unexpectedly.
Use separate names for raw counts, normalized counts and log-transformed values. Transposing a matrix changes the location of the observation dimension; it does not change the biological unit. After filtering, confirm identifiers again rather than relying on the previous check.

title: Programming and reproducible data handling
section: Program with contracts and small functions
text:
Program with contracts and small functions
A function should state what it accepts, what it returns and what assumptions it checks. In a teaching analysis, detecting an unexpected input early is often more useful than making the program silently guess. Positive abundance is required for an ordinary logarithm; an all-missing feature cannot supply a mean or standard deviation.


Show R code
log2_positive <- function(x) {
 stopifnot(is.numeric(x),all(is.finite(x)),all(x>0))
 log2(x)
}
x <- c(2,4,8)
stopifnot(max(abs(2^log2_positive(x)-x))<1e-12)
# Demonstrate rejection without stopping the teaching document.
bad_input <- tryCatch(log2_positive(c(2,0)),error=function(e) 'rejected')
bad_input


[1] "rejected"


This function deliberately disallows missing observations. A different function could support them, but should define their treatment. A successfully returned vector is not evidence that the input measurement was biologically valid.

title: Programming and reproducible data handling
section: Missing values carry information about observation
text:
Missing values carry information about observation
NA is an unknown value, while zero is an observed value on the stated scale. A missing sample, a failed protein identification and a recorded concentration below a detection threshold should not be conflated. A complete-case analysis changes the included population; mean imputation changes variability and covariance.


Show R code
x <- c(3,5,NA,9)
c(observed_n=sum(!is.na(x)),observed_mean=mean(x,na.rm=TRUE))


   observed_n observed_mean 
     3.000000      5.666667 


Show R code
x_zero <- replace(x,is.na(x),0)
c(zero_imputed_mean=mean(x_zero),
 zero_imputed_variance=var(x_zero))


    zero_imputed_mean zero_imputed_variance 
                 4.25                 14.25 


The lower imputed mean follows from a fabricated measurement, not newly acquired evidence. Choose a missingness policy using the assay and question, then report its impact.

title: Programming and reproducible data handling
text:
Make a workflow portable
Use project-relative paths and explicit input/output locations. A clean R session exposes dependencies hidden in an interactive workspace. Functions isolate calculations from unrelated objects, while scripts record the order of operations. Record package versions and data versions; a seed only handles selected random operations.
A command-line program receives arguments as text and should validate their meaning. Filenames containing spaces require appropriate quoting. Capture the exit status of a worker process before reading its outputs. Existing files can be stale after a failed run, so their presence alone does not prove success.
Keep source inputs separate from derived outputs. Do not overwrite the only copy of a measurement table during a transformation. A compact analysis manifest can list each output’s input, transformation and expected row count. Temporary outputs should remain in an explicitly temporary location.






Debugging challenge





An analysis runs interactively but fails in a clean session because normalized is missing. The original session contained an object created manually. Put its creation into the script, state its inputs and verify that the complete workflow runs from the documented starting point.

title: Programming and reproducible data handling
text:
Further reading
Data Carpentry Genomics provides complementary project-organization and command-line lessons. Computational Genomics with R is a broader reference; compare its examples with the explicit keys and units used here.

title: Genomic measurements and sequence analysis
section: Follow the evidence from reads to variants
text:
Follow the evidence from reads to variants
A read is a sampled sequence observation with errors and biases. A reference alignment proposes where it originated; a genotype call combines evidence at a site under a model. These are successive inferences. A base with high reported quality can still map ambiguously, and a confidently mapped read can contain uncertain bases. Distinguish base quality from mapping quality.
Coverage is the number of relevant observations at a position under a counting convention. Mean depth can hide regions with little coverage. PCR duplicates and overlapping mates can affect the amount of independent molecular evidence. Reference divergence and missing sequence can also affect alignment differently across animals.
Genotype dosage counts a specified allele; changing the counted allele from A to B changes dosage from \(g\) to \(2-g\) at a diploid biallelic site. This reverses a regression coefficient’s sign without reversing the underlying biological comparison.


Show R code
gA <- c(0,0,1,1,2,2)
y <- c(2,3,4,5,6,7)
a <- lm(y~gA)
gB <- 2-gA;b <- lm(y~gB)
c(A_effect=coef(a)[2],B_effect=coef(b)[2])


A_effect.gA B_effect.gB 
          2          -2 


Show R code
stopifnot(max(abs(fitted(a)-fitted(b)))<1e-12,
 abs(coef(a)[2]+coef(b)[2])<1e-12)


Record reference and alternate alleles, strand and assembly when joining results. Palindromic allele pairs can be particularly ambiguous without additional frequency and reference information.

title: Genomic measurements and sequence analysis
section: Alignment is an optimization under a scoring rule
text:
Alignment is an optimization under a scoring rule
Global alignment compares whole supplied sequences; local alignment searches for a high-scoring region. Match rewards, mismatch costs and gap costs encode assumptions about what constitutes a useful comparison. Changing them can change the alignment and the reported identity denominator.
A short conserved domain can give high local identity while covering little of the protein. Conversely, global alignment of distant or rearranged sequences may be misleading. Always report alignment coverage and context alongside identity. Low-complexity sequence can match often without supplying strong functional evidence.








Observation
What it supports directly
What remains to investigate




Matching aligned bases
Identity under this alignment
Significance and evolutionary relationship


Similar domain sequence
A candidate domain relationship
Full architecture and functional evidence


Shared variant association
A statistical signal
LD, confounding and causal allele


Supported tree branch
A relationship under the tree model
Alignment/model sensitivity and gene/species histories

title: Genomic measurements and sequence analysis
text:
Distances, saturation and phylogenies
Observed mismatches undercount substitutions when a site changes more than once. The Jukes–Cantor correction makes a restrictive equal-rate assumption; its corrected distance rises rapidly near the model boundary. That behavior is a warning about limited information, not evidence of precise very deep divergence.


Show R code
p <- seq(0,.7,length.out=80)
plot(p,-.75*log(1-4*p/3),type='l',
 xlab='Observed mismatch fraction',ylab='JC substitutions per site')
abline(0,1,lty=2,col='grey50')









A distance tree summarizes a supplied dissimilarity matrix under an algorithm. UPGMA assumes an ultrametric structure for its evolutionary interpretation, while other methods have different models. Branch support depends on what is resampled and does not establish that an incorrect model becomes correct. Gene histories can differ from species histories through duplication, recombination and other processes.

title: Genomic measurements and sequence analysis
text:
Quality decisions need denominators
For an assay summary, record the number of positions or samples assessed. A genotype call rate is the fraction called among eligible observations; a high call rate does not certify correct calls. Filtering can remove poor measurements but can also change the set of variants or animals represented.
Before linking a sequence result to biology, inspect reference coverage, sample quality and annotation. Confirm whether the inference concerns the observed region, the full gene or an organism relationship. A pipeline ending with a neat table still requires those distinctions.






Interpretation challenge





Two proteins share 95% identity over 20 residues but each has 500 residues. Is their overall function established? No. Assess alignment coverage, domain architecture, complexity and biological evidence; a short region supplies a limited claim.
